Volume IX of the Commentary on the *Mūlakarma-sūtra*:
Entering the Wisdom of the Dharma-limit (*dharmānta-jñāna*). This refers to the forty kinds of eloquence (*pratibhāna*), by which one skillfully enters all dharmas through various forms of eloquence.
Because it is the limit of differentiation, it is called "the wisdom that enters the limit of phenomena" (*dharmatā-paryanta-jñāna*).

Regarding the "forty eloquences," this is because the four unhindered knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) possess ten types [of aspects]. As the *Daśabhūmika-bhāṣya* states: "These four unhindered knowledges have ten kinds of distinctions: first, based on specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*);

second, based on common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*); third, the aspect of practice (*ākāra*); fourth, the aspect of exposition; fifth, the aspect of knowledge; sixth, the aspect of freedom from pride (*nirmāna*); seventh..."

The characteristics of the Hīnayāna and Mahāyāna; the characteristics of the eight bodhisattva stages; the characteristics of the stage of the Tathāgata; and the characteristics of the stage of activity and abiding. Regarding the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), there are four:
first, the specific characteristic of the production of phenomena; second, the specific characteristic of differentiation; third, the specific characteristic of the firmness of conceptualization;

and fourth, the specific characteristic of the differentiation of those conceptualizations. As the Sūtra says: "This bodhisattva, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of dharmas (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), knows all..."
Because of the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena, one knows the differentiated characteristics of all phenomena through the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*).

Because of the indestructible exposition of all phenomena, one knows them through the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*). Because of the uninterrupted succession of all phenomena, one knows them through the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*).
There are four kinds of common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*): first, the common characteristic of all phenomena; second, [the common characteristic] of all that exists...

[They share] the same characteristic. Third, all phenomena share the same characteristic of being conventional designations (*prajñapti*). Fourth, conventional designations share the same characteristic of being conventional designations. As the Sūtra says:
"Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature;

by means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one knows the characteristics of the arising of the meanings of all phenomena; by means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one knows that all phenomena are merely conventional designations..."

Because it explains by severing the teaching on dharmas that are merely conventional designations. This is because, through the unimpeded knowledge of following speech, one explains the boundless dharmas that remain unimpaired according to conventional designations;
and so forth, as explained at length.

Next, regarding the statement that "all meritorious practices are fully accomplished": this is because within these forty gates of eloquence (*pratibhāna*), there are no virtuous qualities that are not subsumed.
Regarding the phrase "the habitual tendencies of the mind have already ceased and ignorance is also eliminated":

this stage is called the Stage of Mastery over the Mind (*citta-vaśitā-bhūmi*), because the heavy habitual tendencies of attachment to the mind have been severed and extinguished. [Those who] act while remaining within the ignorance of abiding in this stage are deluded.
Because even the emptiness of mind has been eliminated. Regarding "the treasury of all Buddhas": by means of various *dhāraṇīs*, one attains the treasury of the Dharma of all Buddhas.
As that sutra states: "The ninth Bodhisattva stage is named 'Attaining the Treasury of the Dharma of All Buddhas.
One is able to act as a great Dharma teacher, attaining the *dhāraṇī* of manifold meanings and the *dhāraṇī* of manifold dharmas, up until the fulfillment of the ten [stages]."
Because of the hundreds of thousands of *koṭis* of *dhāraṇī* gates;

as for the "Treasury of All Transformative Powers," it is because he has attained the sovereign power of the light of Dharma, whereby he performs transformations throughout the ten directions. As that sutra says:
"This bodhisattva pervades unspeakably unspeakable worlds, teaching the Dharma according to their minds, according to their faculties, and according to their inclinations. He attains...
Because of the illumination of the Dharma, one seeks the powers of the Tathāgata to fulfill the Buddha-work and to serve as a refuge for all sentient beings.

From "immeasurable" onwards, this further elucidates the contemplation of the ten unhindered knowledges mentioned in the preceding sentence; that is to say, the immeasurable rain of the Dharma-clouds.

Regarding the phrase "pouring down upon all sentient beings," the meaning of the Dharma-cloud (*dharmameghā*) is briefly twofold: first, its ability to receive the immeasurable rain of Dharma from all Buddhas;
second, its ability to pour down the immeasurable rain of Dharma upon sentient beings. Here, the Dharma-cloud is elucidated according to the latter sense.
As that sutra states: "O Son of the Buddha, when a bodhisattva dwells in this stage of the Dharma-cloud, by virtue of their own power of vows..."

Raising the great cloud of loving-kindness and shaking the thunderous roar of the Great Dharma, he takes the brilliance of unimpeded wisdom as his lightning and the light of great insight as his swift wind;
with the roots of merit from great fortune as the dense original clouds, he manifests various physical forms to obstruct the clouds of defilement and pours down the rain of the True Dharma.
In a single thought-moment, he destroys all demonic adversaries—immeasurable and boundless.

It likewise pervades hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of worlds, pouring down the great Dharma-rain of the roots of goodness—the nectar of the Dharma—to extinguish the dust and heat of the afflictions arising from ignorance that sentient beings experience according to their inclinations;

for this reason, this stage is called the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*). As for the phrase "the two habitual tendencies of ignorance are now completely extinguished," it refers to mastery over both form and mind.
This stage increases further because the two subtle habitual tendencies have been exhausted and fundamental ignorance has also attained cessation.
Regarding the one who receives the great position, as that sūtra states: "The bodhisattva practices in accordance with such wisdom and enters the stage of receiving the position;
he immediately attains the name 'Bodhisattva,' and the Samādhi Free from Defilement manifests before him," continuing thus up to ten asaṃkhyeyas.
A hundred thousand samādhis arise, and finally, the samādhi named "Attaining the Supreme State of All-Knowledge Wisdom" manifests before him.
Immediately, a great jewel-lotus king appears, its circumference equaling ten *asaṃkhyeya* hundreds of thousands of triple-thousand great thousandfold world systems;
this is as explained at length in the scriptures. Thus, his supernatural powers are immeasurable and cannot be fully described, manifesting in accordance with reality.
Regarding the phrase "because of the Buddha’s signless activity," as that sūtra states:

"Abiding in this Bodhisattva stage of the Cloud of Dharma, throughout all realms—from descending from Tuṣita Heaven, entering the womb, dwelling in the womb, up to the Great Parinirvāṇa—all Buddha-activities are performed according to the beings to be saved.
Having attained mastery over wisdom, [this extends] even unto hundreds of thousands of asaṃkhyeya worlds."
...and so on, as explained at length.

Thus, the second summary below refers to the "Ten Stages" (*Daśabhūmika*) chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. Within the section on the Stainless Stage (*Vimalā-bhūmi*), the text consists of three parts:
first, the mind; second, the practice; and third, the summary. The first is called the "mind of entering the Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu-praveśa-citta*). It enters...
Because it is the initial gateway to the single dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and because it serves as the skillful means for the ultimate path.
Next, the practice is explained in two parts: first, the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) which is the basis; second, the practice which depends upon it.

Regarding the first, "the concentration of courageous subduing" (*vīrya-parākrama-samādhi*) is so called because it can subdue the obstacles to be abandoned at the stage of Buddhahood. From this concentration, one enters the *dharmāloka-samādhi* and ascends...

The summit of the mountain of the *dharmadhātu*, because it illuminates all *dharmadhātus*. Next, regarding the practice that depends [upon this], there is a general indication followed by a specific explanation.
If one correlates the three stages according to the previous explanation, this section clarifies the meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that serves as the basis;

it pertains to the stage of a hundred *kalpas*, for it is said that one dwells for a hundred *kalpas* while cultivating a thousand *samādhis*. Among the ten specific explanations, the first four dharmas pertain to the stage of a thousand *kalpas*. Regarding that...
It is said that for a thousand kalpas, one dwells in life while training in the Buddha’s majestic deportment and even the methods of spiritual transformation through supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).

As for the latter six dharmas, they pertain to the stage of ten thousand kalpas; therein, it is said that one dwells in life for ten thousand kalpas, manifests as a Buddha, and enters the Great Samādhi of Quiescence.
The Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas transcend the realms of the two truths; they are neither existent nor non-existent, without mind and without form.
Regarding the two habits of cause and effect, there is no habituation remaining whatsoever. They manifest as identical to the ancient Buddhas, possessing only names corresponding to their functions.

They manifest various forms and minds to teach and transform sentient beings, constantly practicing the Middle Way of great bliss and unconditionedness. Because arising and ceasing constitute a distinction, among the four preceding [categories], [this is the case].
The third, "repeatedly practicing the dharmas previously performed," refers to the two preceding gates; since emulating the Buddha's virtues is difficult to accomplish, one practices them repeatedly.
The fourth, "inquiry after well-being," is also subsumed under training in the Buddha’s majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*). Regarding the fifth, "parting from the parents of ignorance":
because one has not yet been born into the Buddha-ground, one now parts from them first; at this stage, one still remains with ignorance.

Because they are both present. Regarding the "Gate of the Double Profundity of the Six Entrances" (ṣaḍāyatana): this refers to the gate of emptiness-of-emptiness (śūnyatā-śūnyatā), which is called the double profundity.

This gate of emptiness-of-emptiness is that which only a Buddha can fully exhaust; now, having attained a small portion of it, it is called an "entrance. Regarding the seventh, "manifesting in common with the Buddhas by manifesting all forms and characteristics":

this means manifesting in common with the ancient Buddhas by manifesting all material forms (rūpa) and mind (citta). Regarding the eighth, "being fully endowed with the two kinds of Dharma-body": [this is as follows].
Because one has attained fulfillment within the practice of the cause. Ninth, "the two habit-energies of duality do not exist":
because the two habit-energies of cause and effect are without remainder. Grasping at phenomena (*dharma*) is the cause; grasping at a person (*pudgala*) is the fruit.

Since both of these habitual perfusions have been severed, this is spoken with reference to the final moment of thought; prior to this, there is still a remainder. Tenth, "ascending to the Middle Way of the Ultimate Truth."
Regarding "the summit of the truths" (*satya-śikhara*): this refers to the Middle Way revealed by the preceding four gates.
Because one attains the summit at this stage, the following second section provides a summary in four points: first, citing prior practices; second, manifesting present virtues.

Third, the previous detailed exposition is indicated; fourth, the present abbreviated exposition is concluded. Within the first [section], there are two parts: first, a general enumeration of the forty minds;
second, a specific enumeration of the bodies of the ten stages (*bhūmi*). The fortieth among these forty minds is the stage of the noble ones (*ārya*), for it possesses two bodies.

From the passage "having passed through hundreds of thousands of kalpas" below, it follows that the virtues of the present [stage] likewise pass through ten thousand kalpas, yet this is merely a brief mention. Third...
Regarding the detailed exposition shown [in this text], the third dhyāna does not appear in this assembly within the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*; it should be found in the main body of that sūtra.
As for the fourth abbreviated exposition, its textual characteristics can be understood [by the reader].
The stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) also consists of three parts: first, the mind; second, the qualities (*guṇa*); and third, the concluding clarification.

Regarding the first, it speaks of the "mind of quiescence" because it is the wisdom of tranquil illumination. Following the stage of wondrous enlightenment, the second part manifests its qualities. Briefly stated, there are four qualities:
first, the quality of permanence; second, the quality of wisdom; third, the quality of inconceivability; and fourth, the quality of abiding alone in non-duality. Regarding the first of these:

The stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) is so called because it is far removed from all coarse defilements and because it is free from all ignorance and its latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
It is eternally abiding in a single aspect (*ekalakṣaṇa*) because it is devoid of arising and ceasing, and lacks any distinction between before and after. It is the foremost and unsurpassed.

It is without beginning and without end; it is without middle and without limit, for it is boundless whether viewed vertically or horizontally. It is by virtue of this meaning that it is as profound and still as empty space.
Regarding the term "omniscient wisdom" (*sarvākārajñatā*) mentioned in the second section, this refers generally to the Tathāgata’s wisdom capable of illumination.

Below, it is specifically revealed in four parts: first, the gate of the two truths; second, the gate of beginning and end; third, the gate of defilement (*saṃkleśa*); [and fourth, the gate of purification].
The Gate of Cause and Effect. The Gate of the Fourfold Purity of Cause and Effect. Regarding the first, "non-arising" refers to the realization of the truth of non-existence (*asatya*).

Regarding "the beginning and end of existence," this refers to the illumination of the truth of existence (*satya*). Taking that which has no beginning as the beginning, and that which has no end as the end—this is spoken of as having a beginning and an end merely as a provisional designation to manifest the ultimate limit of illumination.
Regarding the second, the phrase "the root of sentient beings" refers to the four stages of abiding (*catvāraḥ nivāsabhūmayaḥ*). "Having a beginning" refers to...
Because the Tathāgatagarbha is its root, that which has an end consists of the two kinds of birth-and-death as its branches;

this shall be further analyzed in the subsequent passage. Regarding the mention of "knowing in a single thought-moment" in the third and fourth [sections], the Tathāgata truly has no distinction between preceding and succeeding thoughts;
it is simply that the impermanent wisdom of this bodhisattva, within the duration of a single thought-moment, is such that the Buddha can—

Because of thorough knowledge. Regarding the statement in the third quality that the Buddha "dwells in the inconceivable," this is because there are five kinds of inconceivability regarding the Buddha’s dwelling in unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*). As stated in the *Anuttarāśrayasūtra*:

"All Tathāgatas, dwelling in the state of unsurpassed enlightenment, possess five kinds of causes and conditions that are inconceivable. What are these five? First, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); second..."
...this locus. Third, abiding; fourth, as being identical or different; fifth, for the sake of benefit. How is it that the Tathāgata’s self-nature of bodhi is inconceivable?
One cannot find the Tathāgata in form (*rūpa*); one cannot find the Tathāgata apart from form.

It is the same for feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). It is likewise for the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). It is likewise for existence...
Dharmas are unattainable as the Tathāgata; non-dharmas are likewise so. This is called the inconceivable intrinsic nature of bodhi.
Why is the locus of the Tathāgata’s bodhi inconceivable? The Tathāgata abiding in the desire realm is inconceivable;
his departure from the desire realm is inconceivable; it is likewise for the form and formless realms. The six destinies and the ten...
The directions are likewise thus. This is called the inconceivability of location. What is the inconceivability of abiding?
The Tathāgata’s abiding in the dwelling of peace and bliss is inconceivable. The Tathāgata’s abiding in the dwelling of tranquility is inconceivable.
Likewise, the Tathāgata’s abiding with mind, the Tathāgata’s abiding without mind, and the Tathāgata’s abiding in the Brahma-dwellings are all inconceivable. In what sense are they one or different?
It is inconceivable that the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time abide in a single place. What is this single place?
It is the self-nature pure, untainted *dharmadhātu*. Whether these Tathāgatas are one or many is inconceivable.
How is it that their activities for the benefit of others are inconceivable? The wisdom, spiritual powers, and divine faculties of the Tathāgatas are all equal within the single *dharmadhātu*.
Abiding in the untainted, pure dharma-realm, one is able to bring immeasurable benefit to sentient beings; this is called inconceivable benefit.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of inconceivability: first, it is ineffable, because it transcends the realm of language;
second, it transcends all worlds, because there is nothing in the world that can serve as a simile for it. This...
It is because it is named "inconceivable. Regarding the fourth virtue, the statement that it exists alone in non-duality beyond the two truths is as stated in the *Rājanirdeśa-sūtra*:
"Transcending both worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) and ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), it constitutes the omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) of the eleventh stage;

it realizes that while phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent, they are nonetheless pure. As for what is called "worldly truth," it refers to the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).

Regarding the nature [of phenomena], there are the two truths of existence and non-existence. Within this context, these are combined as the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is absent;

that which is revealed [by its absence] is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), namely suchness (*tathatā*). The Tathāgata returns to the source of the one mind, which is neither existent nor non-existent.
It is neither false nor real; neither conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); neither differentiated nor equal.
Therefore, it is said that beyond the two truths lies a third truth, peerless and without counterpart, called the "Non-dual Truth" and the "Inexhaustible Truth.

Thus, it is said to abide alone in non-duality. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "By the power of faith and understanding, one knows [this], yet it is not attained through the wisdom of the inexhaustible truth."

Therefore, from "My former [teachings]" below, the third section concludes by clarifying the meaning. First, it points to the detailed exposition; subsequently, it concludes the abbreviated exposition.
Above, the first part correctly elucidated the virtues of practice; from here on, the second part consists of various categorical distinctions, which contains two sections.
First there is the question, followed by the answer. Regarding the phrase "the subsequent stage" within the question, this refers to the Tathāgata-stage.
As for the "Dharmatā-body," it is so called because true wisdom arises in dependence upon the Dharmatā; thus, it is named after its basis as the "Dharmatā[-body].
The passage below refers to the "Dharmatā-dharmakāya," which is precisely this body.
The answer consists of six parts: first, the gate of the world; second, the gate of worldly fruits; third, the gate of the remedies; fourth, the gate of the objects to be remedied;

fifth, the gate of the two births; and sixth, the gate of the two karmas. Within the first [part], there are three sections: first, the manifestation of the two bodies; second, the manifestation of the two lands;
and third, the repeated manifestation of body and land. Within the first of these, there are two subsections: a general heading and a detailed explanation. The meaning is as previously explained.
The textual structure is clear. Within the section on the two lands, there are three parts: the introduction, the explanation, and the conclusion. Within the explanation, there are two sections:
first, a simultaneous manifestation of the land of ordinary beings; second, a formal clarification of the land of noble beings. This [second section] contains two further divisions:

first, the land of bodhisattvas; second, the land of Tathāgatas. Therefore, the following portion constitutes the third part, the conclusion. From "the single thought-moment of the first stage" onwards is the third layer of clarification.
It is profoundly deep. Within it there are three aspects: first, the profundity of the two bodies; second, the profundity of the dharma-body;
and third, the profundity of cause and effect. Regarding the first of these, there are two parts: first, clarifying that it is immeasurable; second, revealing its provisional designations.

Within the section on provisional designations, the mention of "a hundred bodies, a thousand bodies, ten thousand bodies, and so forth" in the first stage refers to a thousand bodies in the second stage and ten thousand bodies in the third stage, and so on. There is...

Regarding "there is bondage, yet there is liberation": the fruit of the retribution of grasping is limited to a hundredfold number; therefore, it is said that there is bondage. The fruit of the wisdom of vows transcends all numerical limits;

therefore, it is said that there is liberation. Furthermore, in view of what has not yet been severed, it is said that there is bondage; in view of what has already been severed, it is said that there is liberation.
As for the second section on the profound nature of the Dharmakāya, there are two parts within it.
First, the non-perception of wisdom through principle (*li-zhi*) is clarified; subsequently, the perception of wisdom through cognition (*liang-zhi*) is revealed.

It may also be said that the third section below concerns the profound depth of cause and effect. Within this, there are three parts: first, the provisional designation of having causes and having effects is clarified; the three stages of worthiness (*san-xian*) constitute the cause.

Because the wondrous enlightenment is the fruit, it is next explained that the causal and fruitional states transcend words, while the path of transformation is provisionally described. "You should [practice]" constitutes the third section, the conclusion and exhortation.
Within the second section, the worldly fruits, there are two parts: the citation, the explanation, and the conclusion. Within the second part, the explanation, there are fifteen items.
The Stages. Within each of the first four stages, there are five points: first, adornment; second, royal station; third, retinue;

fourth, the place of receiving instruction; and fifth, the place of teaching and transforming. Within the latter eleven [stages], there are only four points. Regarding the "copper-jewel necklace" in the first stage:
it is a metaphor for adorning the body with the adornments of the ten stages of practice (*daśabhūmi*). Regarding the "king of the copper wheel": when receiving the royal station, the copper...
Because he responds to the turning of the wheel [of Dharma]. Regarding "having meritorious sons": the king has one hundred sons, all of whom possess merit and virtue;

thus they are born in a single Buddha-field to practice the teachings of the Buddha, for they are born simultaneously in a single Buddha-world. Regarding "teaching two continents": [the king teaches] these two continents.
Because he acts as a king over two continents, the five subsequent phrases should be understood accordingly.
Regarding the statement in the third [stage] that one "enters the lands of the Buddhas of the ten directions," it means that one attains birth in ten Buddha-worlds simultaneously.

As for the four heavenly kings in the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* states that they mostly act as kings of Jambudvīpa; this is the place where the Buddha attained enlightenment.
He was born for the purpose of establishing the Buddha-dharma; as for the mention here of the Four Great Kings, it is because their respective levels correspond to this location.
Therefore, both textual accounts are logical. Other divergent interpretations should be understood accordingly.
The "necklace of a thousand jewels" refers to those below the second stage; the "necklace of ten thousand jewels" refers to those below the third stage;

and so on, up to the King of the Three Realms at the level of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). This is because he also transforms sentient beings of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), as he is born in the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

As stated in the *Daśabhūmika-vibhaṅga-sūtra*: the Buddha said, "I shall explain to you the formless concentrations (*ārūpyasamādhi*). [Regarding] the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*)...
What is called "form" (rūpa): that which lacks such form is called "formless" (arūpya). Now, form consists of the five [aggregates] which constitute the four great elements;

it is only because they lack visible form that they are called "formless. The form of sensation (vedanā), the form of mental formations (saṃskāra), and the form of consciousness (vijñāna) are not seen by ordinary beings with the five supernatural powers (pañcābhijñā).
Only the Tathāgata and the irreversible Bodhisattvas see those forms. The irreversible Bodhisattva maintains them.
Through skillful means, he travels to the heavens of those with perception and preaches the subtle Dharma to their faint consciousnesses.

Regarding the phrase "the King of the Dharma-realm within wondrous awakening," it is because he universally transforms sentient beings throughout the boundless Dharma-realm. From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards is the third summary.
As for "moving and resting together," it is because the external sign of the precious wheel follows the King as they travel together, constantly accompanying his person.
This is because the inner practice of the *adornment* (*mālā*) constantly accords with the two bodies.

Within the third section, the "Gate of the Antidotes," there are two parts: a specific explanation and a general manifestation. Regarding the statement that "the Bodhisattvas of the Three Stages of Worthiness (*trayaḥ-pudgalāḥ*) subdue the coarse karmic paths of the afflictions of the three realms":
they have already subdued the delusions arising from discrimination within the three realms, and they also subdue [the causes of] the evil destinies.
Because of wholesome karma, even though the fruits of continuity may arise as coarse, the fruits of the eight difficulties do not arise.
This refers to the joyous patience (*kṣānti*) of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), which subdues the karmic paths of the three realms by severing the seeds of the karma of the three evil realms;

however, because one has not yet abandoned fundamental ignorance (*mūlāvidyā*), it is termed "subduing. This same explanation applies to all instances of subduing in the higher stages. [This concerns] the first stage (*bhūmi*).
Regarding the two types of ignorance within the obstacles [of the first stage], the second is the ignorance of karma pertaining to the evil realms.

As for "the karma of the human realm among those who have abandoned patience and are subdued," this refers to the karma of humans because various subtle transgressions of the precepts frequently arise among those in the human realm; thus it is called "human karma.

Regarding the two types of ignorance within the obstacles of the second stage, the second is the ignorance of various karmic activities. This clarifies the subduing of the six [realms] through patience.
Regarding the karmic paths of the heavens: within the six heavens of the desire realm, there is the differentiation of the five desires.

Because these obstruct the practice of the superior meditative concentration of the third bhūmi, and because all such obstructions below this point are collectively termed "karma" due to their association with volitional mental factors (*cetanā*), among the two types of obstructions to the third bhūmi:
The first is the delusion of sensual desire. Regarding the phrase "the blazing patience that subdues the karmic paths of various views":

this refers to grasping at the literal meaning of the teachings, which obstructs the practice and conduct of the fourth stage (*bhūmi*). Among the two types of obstacles to the fourth stage, the second is the ignorance caused by craving for the subtle and pure Dharma.
Regarding the phrase "the supreme patience that subdues the karmic paths of doubt and views": it is for the purpose of entering...
Regarding birth and death, one hesitates whether to enter nirvana; thus, it is called the view of doubt.

Among the two obstacles of the fifth stage, the first is the mental state of desiring to enter nirvana while simultaneously desiring to enter birth and death—this is the ignorance of conceptualization.
"Presently enduring and subduing the path of cause and effect" refers to discerning the characteristics of the twelve links of dependent origination. This is the obstacle of the sixth stage.

Within these two [categories], the first is the ignorance (*avidyā*) that manifests as the continuity of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Regarding the patience of non-arising (*anutpattikadharmakṣānti*) which subdues the karmic path of results:

it refers to the discrimination of the three phases of a momentary result-phenomenon. Among the two [patiences] of the seventh stage, the first is the ignorance regarding whether subtle marks appear or do not appear.
The patience of immovability (*aniñjyakṣānti*) subdues the karma of the cause of form (*rūpa*), while the patience of light (*ābhāsakṣānti*) subdues the mind.

Regarding the "causal path of karma" (*hetu-karmapatha*): it refers to the manifest activity of conceptualization that clings to form and mind; because it is capable of perfuming seeds, it is designated as the "cause.

Because it never again manifests, it is termed "subdued" (*vibhava*). Among the two [types of obstacles] within the eighth and ninth stages, both take the second, the obstacle of ignorance (*avidyā-āvaraṇa*).

Through the patience of quiescent extinction (*śānti-kṣānti*), one subdues the two habitual tendencies of mind and form; through the stainless patience (*vimala-kṣānti*), one subdues the path and its fruit.

Regarding "cultivation": because one can sever the latencies (*vāsanā*) of the two attachments in the tenth stage, and because one can abandon the heavy impediments (*dauṣṭhulya*) of the two attachments in the Stainless Stage (*vimalā-bhūmi*), the heavy impediments—which arise from those manifest causes and latencies and continue without interruption—are said to be their fruit.
However, speaking in terms of ultimate reality, they are severed in each and every stage.

There are three types. However, because one wishes to demonstrate that their capacity to counteract [the afflictions] becomes increasingly profound, they are described in the order of cause, subsequent practice, and final fruit.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of *dauṣṭhulya* (gross heaviness): first, the *dauṣṭhulya* belonging to the category of afflictions, which is simultaneously severed when its seeds are eliminated;

second, the *dauṣṭhulya* belonging to the category of maturation (*vipāka*), which, though of the same nature as the former, is subtle and attenuated, and whose continuity does not cease even after its seeds have been eliminated.

Therefore, it is said that although the prior habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have already been extinguished, the fruit does not perish. Now, by abandoning these [tendencies], one subdues the fruit of the habitual tendencies.
For this reason, the following section provides a general clarification. It establishes three stages in total to clarify subduing and severing:

during the Three Stages of Worthiness (*triyāna*), there is only subduing, as one has not yet attained vision; within the eleven stages (*bhūmi*), there is both subduing and severing, because the root has not yet been uprooted; and once the seeds have been severed...

Therefore, within the patience of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue ren*), there is only severance and no suppression, because fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*) has already been eternally exhausted.

As for all ignorance within the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), this refers to the ignorance that arises within the maturation-consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*); among these, one attains Buddhahood and severs them instantaneously.
Hence, it is said to be "instantaneous severance. A detailed explanation of this will be provided in the subsequent text.
Below this is the fourth section, the gate of the delusions to be remedied. This section contains two parts: first, the cause; second, the result.
Within the cause, there is both a detailed explanation and a summary. In the detailed explanation, the fundamental ignorance is first clarified:

"Not comprehending all phenomena, one becomes deluded regarding the dharma-dhātu and gives rise to the karmic results of the three realms. This means not comprehending that all phenomena are in fact the single dharma-dhātu, as explained in the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra*.
The treatise states: "Because one does not penetrate the single dharma-realm, the mind is non-concordant; that a thought suddenly arises is termed ignorance.
Next, it clarifies the secondary branches. Among these, the mention of "the view of precept-clinging" refers precisely to the grasping of precepts, as it involves calculating [false causes].

The "view of grasping at results" (*phaladṛṣṭi*) is precisely the "clinging to views" (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*), because it conceives of false results; that is to say, it conceives of saṃsāra as being pleasant, pure, and so forth.

Furthermore, it is called the "view of results" because it is satisfied with what is superior. These two types are termed "views of grasping" (*parāmarśadṛṣṭi*), because the sense of "grasping" (*parāmarśa*) refers to a false apprehension.
As for the "view of doubt" (*vicikitsādṛṣṭi*), it is the investigation of principles through hesitant discernment; thus, it is a form of discerning wisdom (*prajñā*).
It is called "view" (*dṛṣṭi*). Because hesitant wisdom is characterized by doubt, in order to clarify this meaning, it is said that there are seven views;

they are called "views" because they seek out every object. Regarding the statement that there are six types of "attachment" (*sakti*), greed is divided into three: because it obstructs the supreme cause for the path of renunciation (*nairyāṇika-mārga*).
Sexual desire is termed "lust" (*kāma*); the rest are termed "craving" (*tṛṣṇā*). Attachment to present objects is termed "greed" (*lobha*); longing for the past is termed "craving."

The longing for the future is collectively termed *tṛṣṇā* (craving). Furthermore, that which arises directed toward external objects within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is termed *rāga* (greed), while that which arises directed toward internal objects within the form and formless realms (*rūpadhātu* and *ārūpyadhātu*) is termed *tṛṣṇā*.
That which arises at all times within the sphere of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*) is as it has been said:
The thirteen types of perfuming flow continuously and without interruption within the *vipāka-vijñāna*.

Therefore, this consciousness is called the "Dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*), because it can sustain the seeds of all phenomena within the three realms; "realm" (*dhātu*) carries the meanings of "sustaining" and "cause.
From the words "O Son of the Buddha" onwards is the second summary. Regarding the statement that "all afflictions have these thirteen as their basis," among the secondary afflictions (*upakleśa*):

Since both the great and the small [categories of ignorance] take these thirteen as their fundamental basis, and because the ground of abiding ignorance serves as the root for these thirteen, the following section clarifies the delusions regarding the fruits.
This consists of three parts: a general heading, a detailed explanation, and [the conclusion].

The subsequent section clarifies their mutual inclusion. In the detailed explanation, the mention of "the two karmas of views and attachment" refers to the karma produced by the two afflictions of views and attachment.

Such afflictions and karma are sustained by the deluded *vipākavijñāna* (maturation-consciousness). The retributive portion arising from the mind and mental factors of form and desire constitutes the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).
If one is free from sexual desire, the retributive portion arising from the mind and mental factors of form and delusion constitutes the Form [Realm] (*rūpadhātu*).

Regarding the realms (*dhātu*): if one is free from craving for form (*rūpa-rāga*), yet is deluded by the retribution arising from the meditative mind, this constitutes the formless realm (*ārūpya-dhātu*).
Therefore, within the classification of inclusion by these lower characteristics, there are two parts: first, clarifying inclusion; second, revealing non-inclusion.

Regarding the first, the statement that "nothing is excluded from the dharma-realm" (*dharma-dhātu*) means that all things are subsumed within the matured consciousness (*vipāka-vijñāna*). Regarding the second, it says "only the Buddha... [is not so included].

Regarding "one person exiting outside the dharma-realm": this is because only a Buddha can be separated from the *vipāka-vijñāna* (maturation-consciousness). Regarding "coming to enter the treasury of the dharma-realm":
this is because the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment body) enter the triple world; thus, in the *Rājarājasūtra*, it is called the "treasury of the triple world.
It says that the afflictions of all sentient beings do not arise, and they exit the treasury of the triple world; the retributions of all sentient beings [are] twenty...
The two roots do not transcend the triple world (*tridhātu*). The *dharmakāya* manifested by the Buddhas likewise does not transcend the triple world.

Outside the triple world, there are no sentient beings; if so, whom would the Buddhas transform? Therefore, I say that outside the triple world there exists separately a "storehouse of the realm of sentient beings.
This is taught in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), and was not spoken by the seven Buddhas. This meaning is fully explained as follows.

The Chapter on the Path explains this. Below, the fifth section clarifies the two types of birth. This contains two parts: a detailed explanation and a summary. Within the detailed explanation, there are two further divisions:

first, the clarification of birth through karma; second, the manifestation of birth through transformation. Within the category of birth through karma, there are also two distinctions: [the first concerns] the stage of the three levels of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*).

Having subdued coarse ignorance, one is freed from the karma of bondage; yet there remains the function of subtle craving, because it does not consist of bound karma. Regarding "the seeds of goodness acting as conditions":

this is because the seeds of retributive causes serve as the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*). Regarding "craving moistening karma": this is because active craving moistens the seeds of karma.
Thus, it is said that "the function is stilled while the function of craving is not severed," meaning that the function of bound karma is stilled.
They differ from ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) because their craving moistens karma; they differ from later noble ones (*ārya*) because [their defilements are not yet exhausted].

Next, the statement that "eleven types of persons also suppress the karmic fruits of the three realms within the dharma-realm" (*dharmadhātu*) refers collectively to the stages of the noble ones. From the first stage (*bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage, the fruits of the three realms are all suppressed and exhausted without remainder;
the statement that they are "exhausted at the eighth stage" clarifies that in this stage, birth by means of karma is eliminated through principle (*nyāya*).
Because they are born through mastery over the power of their vows, they do not give rise to craving to moisten karma. Even up to the seventh bhūmi, craving no longer arises;

in their final body, they do not undergo further rebirth, and thus it is said that there is "no remainder. In the eighth bhūmi, they do not undergo [rebirth], and thus it is said that [craving] is "exhausted.
From this point upward, they manifest as Buddhas. Below this is the second section, which clarifies birth through transformation (nirmāṇa); that is, from the eighth...
From the [first] stage upward through the four stages, one does not receive the retribution of the seeds of karma belonging to the three realms;
therefore, it is said that there is no "love for children" regarding the retribution of the three realms, because the afflictions of the three realms have all been suppressed and exhausted.

However, because the ignorance of clinging to phenomena (*dharmagrāha-avidyā*) has not yet been suppressed and exhausted, it is said that only the habitual tendencies of ignorance remain. By the power of this ignorance of clinging to phenomena, one generates uncontaminated karma (*anāsrava-karma*) and undergoes [rebirth].
Regarding the retributive transformation, the seeds of habitual perfuming within the three realms continue without interruption until the stage of the vajra-like samādhi;

therefore, it is said that one has not yet emerged from the three realms. Furthermore, although the wondrous forms upon which the pure land relies are subsumed under the category of untainted dharmas, they all nonetheless rely upon the *vipākavijñāna* (retributive consciousness); for this reason, they are not designated as the "pure land" [in its ultimate sense]. Because...

Regarding those born through the power of great vows and transformations: this refers to taking birth in the palaces of kings within impure lands, as well as undergoing various births within the six realms of existence.
All of these are transformations and do not arise from karma.

For this reason, I previously concluded [the discussion] by stating that "it was taught among the devas," meaning that this principle was taught among the devas of the sixth heaven (*ṣaṣṭha-deva*). As for those born from karma: this refers to those from the seventh stage (*bhūmi*) onwards.
Regarding "returning" and "transformative arising": these refer to the stages from the eighth bhūmi upward.
This concludes the sixth section, which clarifies the two types of karma. Within this, there are two parts: a detailed explanation and a summary.

First, regarding the "wisdom-karma," the phrase "knowledge of signlessness and non-arising" means that because one has forgotten both the signs of conceptual construction (*parikalpita*) and the dependent arising (*paratantra*), every moment of mind takes phenomena as its object.
"Nature" (prakṛti) refers to the realization of the nature of reality (*tattva*). "The arising of non-illumination" occurs because one is free from the conceptualization of grasper and grasped.
Activities such as subduing and severing are also activities of wisdom (*prajñā*), but they have already been explained previously; therefore, they are not mentioned here.

Regarding "wisdom emerging from the truths of existence, which are conditioned and untainted within [the realm of] existence," this refers to the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*) that emerges from the fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*); within this, both [aspects] are present.
Possessing virtues such as compassion, they propagate the Buddha-way above and transform sentient beings below; for this reason, it is collectively termed the "karma of merit.
From the initial stage of sainthood downward, the karma of merit is further elucidated because it is subject to transformation. Regarding the phrase "exhausting the old without creating the new":
as merit increases and shifts from the former to the latter, one is able merely to exhaust the karma of outflows within the cycle of birth and death.
Therefore, no new [birth] is created. As for "transformational birth producing all," although there is birth from karma below the seventh stage, it is also accompanied by transformational birth.

In the "Chapter on Explaining the Meaning," which correctly elucidates the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) within the threefold division, the first part—listing the names—and the second part—discerning their characteristics—are completed above.
This third part, based on the characteristics of contemplative practice, explains the meaning of the aforementioned names; it provides etymological interpretations (*nirukti*) of these various terms.

Therefore, it is titled the "Chapter on Explaining the Meaning. Within the text, there are four sections: the restatement of the question, the promise to explain, the general outline, and the detailed explanation. First, regarding the restatement of the question:

at the beginning of the "Chapter on Training in Contemplation," it asks, "How should a bodhisattva train in contemplating the meaning and characteristics of names, as well as the phenomena that are the objects of the mind?
Furthermore, how should they proceed? Of these two questions, the latter has already been answered; as for the former, the inquiry into "meaning and characteristics," [the text proceeds as follows].
This chapter provides a brief response without extensive explanation; therefore, it now restates the question: "What is the nature of the meaning you previously mentioned?

From the words "That is to say" (*tadyathā*) onwards is the second section, which grants permission to explain the characteristics of the six stages. From the words "O Son of the Buddha" (*jinaputra*) onwards is the third section, which provides a general outline of the essential meaning of what is to be explained.
Regarding the "essence of the Bodhisattva," this refers to the essence of the spiritual lineage (*gotra*). As for the term "merit" (*guṇa*), it is based on...
The spiritual lineage (*gotra*) gives rise to all meritorious qualities; because it possesses great significance and profound rationale, the Buddha provides a second, detailed explanation below.
This explanation of the meaning of the six stages is divided into two parts, as the first three and the latter three constitute these two divisions.

In the explanation of the Three Grades of Worthies (*tri-śukla-kulaputra*), there is a specific clarification and a concluding summary. Within the first ten stages (*daśa-vihāra*), the explanation of the first stage has two parts:

first, clarifying the skillful means for entering the stage; second, explaining the characteristics of the actual entry into the stage. Within the first part, the skillful means, eight phrases are presented:

(1) restating the stage to be entered; (2) citing the person who enters it; (3) the generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*); (4) establishing the name; (5) the practice; (6) ... [text truncated] ... *Note: The provided source text ends abruptly after "六者" (sixth), so the translation reflects this.*
Receiving retribution; seventh, gain and loss; eighth, advancement and retreat. "The Stage of Resolving the Mind" (Cittotpāda-vihāra) refers to that which is entered.

The phrase "this person" and those following identify the one who enters. Regarding the term "those bound by all fetters" (sakalabandhana): they are at the stage of the external ordinary person (bāhyapṛthagjana). "Not knowing" means not recognizing the Three Jewels.
"Not understanding" means not understanding the aspiration for the goal. "Not wise" means being deluded regarding the causes of good and evil. Not... [text ends]

"Knowing" refers to not clearly understanding the fruits of suffering and pleasure. From "ignorance" (*avidyā*) downward, the third section clarifies the arousal of the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*).
"Encountering the teachings of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas" means either encountering a Buddha, or encountering a Bodhisattva, or encountering the teachings of both Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
"Giving rise to even a single thought of faith" means giving rise to decisive faith toward these three objects, believing that the path of the Buddhas exists and is to be cultivated.
Because practice can be attained. Once this faith has been generated, one is said to have entered the stage of the inner ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*). As for the generation of the *bodhicitta*:

it is the generation of a resolute vow toward great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), vowing, "May I attain unsurpassed enlightenment for the sake of accomplishing all the welfare and benefit of all sentient beings.
This refers to the fourth designation established below. Regarding the phrase "at that time": it means after the mind has been generated. Regarding the phrase "abiding": [it refers to] abiding...

The former refers to the period prior to the first stage (*bhūmi*). At that time, one is called a "Bodhisattva of Faith-Imagination" (*śraddhā-saṃjñā-bodhisattva*), because they are able to practice the ten faiths.
They are termed "provisional Bodhisattvas" because their minds are not yet firm or substantial, being like light feathers.

They are termed "nominal Bodhisattvas" because their practice does not correspond to their name, as they have not yet attained the characteristics of the ultimate meaning. Such a person practices the fifth [stage] below.

Within this, there are two parts: first, the elucidation of the ten faiths; second, the manifestation of the ten precepts. As for what are called the "ten wholesome acts," they refer to the abstention from the ten unwholesome acts.

The five, eight, and ten precepts constitute the *saṃvara-śīla* (the morality of restraint). The precepts of the six *pāramitās* constitute the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (the morality of gathering virtuous dharmas).
Furthermore, regarding the sixth [section], the receiving of retribution for those practices below, there are also two parts: first, the restatement of the ten wholesome acts and the ten...

This explains the cause of faith. Subsequently, it reveals the retributions of celestial beings and human kings. A Wheel-turning King of Iron (Cakravartin) governs a single continent, just as the aggregate of form (rūpaskandha) subsumes all forms in general.
A "King of Scattered Millet" (Kṣudra-rāja) separately rules over various kingdoms, just as within the category of elements (dhātu), the ten material elements (rūpa-dhātu) are distinct.
They are called "scattered" because they are like individual grains of millet. If one relies on this meaning, the remaining various kings each govern [their respective domains].
The other kingdoms are all termed "scattered grains. As stated in the *Ratnarāśi Sūtra* (Renwang jing): "Those with superior-grade ten wholesome actions become Iron-Wheel-Turning Kings;
those with middle and inferior grades become scattered-grain kings. In this present sūtra, the scattered-grain kings are divided into two categories.

Those of the middle grade retain their original name, while those of the inferior grade are specifically designated as "human kings" (*manuṣyarāja*), because they have given rise to the great resolve (*mahācitta*).
One attains kingship; because there are distinctions in the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), there are these three differences. Regarding the seventh point below, "possession" and "loss":
although one possesses various afflictions (*kleśa*), one accumulates various roots of goodness. Regarding the eighth point below, "retrogression" and "advancement":
this is first indicated and subsequently explained; the textual structure is clear.

From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the characteristics of the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) are clarified. This section contains two parts: first, the restatement of the preparatory practices (*prayoga*); second, from "beginning to enter" onwards, the actual clarification of the characteristics of the stage.

By means of the gate of the exhaustion of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), the lineage (*gotra*) is made manifest; therefore, it is said: "Beginning to enter the realm of emptiness, one abides in the station of the nature of emptiness.

"Beginning to enter the realm of emptiness" carries the meaning of generating the mind of enlightenment (*cittotpāda*), because one generates the initial mind by relying on the gate of the emptiness of persons. Relying on the person...
The wisdom of emptiness gives rise to practice within existence; by relying on the Buddha’s teachings and through mental attention (*manasikāra*), one cultivates all meritorious qualities.
This is the meaning of "abiding" (*vihāra*). When free from all conceptual discrimination and the mind does not act of its own accord, all meritorious qualities arise spontaneously.
This is the meaning of a "stage" (*bhūmi*). Since this has not yet been attained, it is not called a stage, but is merely termed "abiding. This is the distinction.

"Abiding" (sthiti) and "ground" (bhūmi) are distinct. Regarding the statement in the *Caryā-bhūmi* that one constantly follows the purity of the mind of emptiness through eighty-four thousand dharma-gates:

this refers to purifying that many gates by means of the six perfections (ṣaṭ-pāramitā). This meaning is explained in detail in the *Bhadrapāla-vaipulya-sūtra*. In that [sūtra], there is a bodhisattva...
His name was King of Joy (*Ratnaprabha*). He sat in meditative equipoise for seven days and reflected thus:
"By practicing which samādhi can a bodhisattva swiftly attain the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates of the pāramitās, the dhāraṇī-gates, and so forth?

After the seven days had passed, he went to where the Buddha was and requested instruction on what he had previously contemplated. The Buddha then replied to him: "It is well that you ask about this meaning. There is a gate of samādhi named..."
Having realized the fundamental nature of all phenomena, one practices this samādhi and swiftly attains the eighty-four thousand gates of the pāramitās.
What are these eighty-four thousand? That sūtra states that there are three hundred and fifty kinds of gates to the merits of the Buddhas;
for each of those three hundred and fifty kinds of merit, one cultivates the six pāramitās as their cause.
There are thus two thousand one hundred pāramitās that serve as remedies for the delusions regarding the four great elements and the six decays. There are thus twenty-one thousand pāramitās.
As for the "four great elements," this refers to the internal four great elements. As for the "six decays," this refers to the external six sense objects.
The thieves of the six sense objects (ṣaḍviṣaya) cause the decline and exhaustion of wholesome dharmas; therefore, they are called "declines" (śoka).

Those previous twenty-one thousand perfections (pāramitā), each corresponding to the four types of mental afflictions of sentient beings, thus constitute eighty-four thousand perfections. As for the "four afflictions":
Those with excessive greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as those whose dispositions are equal [in these three], are said to constitute the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates.

Next, it is said that because they are pure and bright, they are called "purifying the ground" (*bhūmi-śodhana*). Relying on the aforementioned eighty-four thousand dharma-gates, one is able to remedy the four great elements, the six decays, and the four afflictions;
thus, the mind-ground becomes clear and white, which is why it is called the stage of "purifying the ground. Regarding the term "long" in the context of cultivation:
Regarding "nurturing all practices": based on the previously cultivated pure and white mind-ground, one nurtures all practices; therefore, it is called "cultivation.
Regarding "being born into nobility," it means being born into the family of the Buddha with a seed-nature that is pure;

because one attains birth in the Buddha-family through the practice performed, and the understanding of emptiness increases further by the power of the Buddha's teaching, it is called "birth into nobility. [One] extensively practices non-...
Regarding the measure of roots of goodness: it refers to skillfully cultivating a multitude of roots of goodness;

for this reason, it is called "perfection of skillful means. Regarding the accomplishment of the sixth [perfection], prajñā: because it counteracts false attachments, it is called "right mind. Regarding entering the realm of ultimate emptiness where there is no arising:
by relying on the power of prajñā, one enters the three types of emptiness with progress and without regression; this is called "non-retrogression."

Furthermore, regarding "not giving rise to inversion from the moment of generating the mind": from the time of first generating the bodhicitta, one remains far removed from inversions and does not give rise to afflictions or demonic influences that could destroy the bodhicitta.
For this reason, it is called "Childlike Purity" (*kumārabhūta*).
It is like a young novice monk who, from birth, has never committed sexual misconduct. As stated in the *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra*, at that time the World-Honored One addressed [the assembly]:
"Aṅgulimāla, you should uphold the pure precepts of a *kumārabhūta* (童真). In the commentary it says: 'Kumārabhūta' is another name for a *śrāmaṇera* (沙彌).
The Indic original is *śikṣā*; in the Song language, it means 'learning,' and also 'conforming without opposition.

That this stage is called 'Kumārabhūta' here is because, from the moment of generating the aspiration [for enlightenment], one conforms to the principles and teachings without any sense of contradiction. You shall succeed to the Buddha."

Regarding "position": because of the power of conformity from the preceding stage of the youthful prince (*kumārabhūta*), one generates understanding through the teachings; thus, one is called a "Dharma Prince" (*dharmarāja-putra*).

Regarding "attaining the supreme mind of non-arising": because this is the most excellent among the understandings of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), it is called "consecration" (*abhiṣeka*).

Within the Ten Practices (*daśa-caryā*), there is first a general clarification: as for "entering the emptiness of the dharma-nature of the five aggregates," in the preceding ten Abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), one attained the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*);

in this stage of the ten Practices, one attains the emptiness of internal dharmas (*adhyātma-dharma-śūnyatā*). Based on the understanding of dharma-emptiness, one also practices the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates;
therefore, they are collectively termed the "Middle Ten Practices. Next, there is a specific clarification regarding the initial entry into dharma-emptiness: the preceding...

Having realized the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), one still maintained [the reality of] phenomena (*dharma*); now that one has realized the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), there is nothing remaining within. For this reason, a mind of joy first arises.

Regarding the second point, it says "constantly transforming sentient beings": because one maintains the practice of the precepts internally and guides sentient beings externally, it is called "benefiting.
"Regarding the actual attainment of the mind of dharma-patience" means attaining the mind of patience regarding the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
By virtue of patience in accordance with the Dharma, one attains patience toward sentient beings; being without "I" or "mine," this is called the absence of malice and resentment.
As for abiding eternally in merit, it is because one’s diligence is unceasing that one abides eternally; because one abides eternally without abandonment, it is called inexhaustible.

Not losing right mindfulness means that by relying on the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), one deeply subdues delusion and distraction; thus, at the time of death, one remains unturbid. Therefore...
This is called being free from delusion and confusion. As for "being ever-present in every birth," it is because through the power of *prajñā*, one accords with the Awakened One;
thus, one is constantly manifest in birth within Buddha-lands, and is therefore named "Sudr̥śa" (Well-Appearing).

As for "non-self within the self," it is by relying on the power of skillful means (*upāya*) that one skillfully departs from the two extremes, such that there is no defilement or attachment toward any phenomena; therefore, he is named "Asaṅga" (Non-Attached). He is always in accord with...
"Veneration" means that by relying on the power of the *praṇidhāna-pāramitā*, one is always able to accord with the Buddhadharma of the three periods of time; hence it is called "respect.

"Expounding the Dharma to deliver beings" means that by relying on the power of the *bala-pāramitā*, one moves and establishes the norms for all things, causing them to abandon evil and practice good; hence it is called "wholesome Dharma."
Regarding the statement that "the two truths are not as they appear": it is not because the words "two" imply that there are actually two things as they appear;

therefore, they are said to be "not as they appear. Why is this so? Because they are neither characterized by marks (*lakṣaṇa*) nor devoid of marks. Because they are not characterized by marks, they do not exist as the expression "truths with marks";

because they are not devoid of marks, they do not exist as the designation "truths without marks. To understand them in this way is to be free from false speech. For this reason, [it is said that the two truths are not as they appear].

This is called "True Practice" (*bhūtacaryā*). Its name is established based on the *Prajñāpāramitā* (Perfection of Wisdom). If one asks what difference there is between this and the aforementioned *Prajñāpāramitā* (Perfection of Insight):

the former clarifies the elimination of marks (*nimitta*) to enter emptiness in accordance with the meaning of the Buddha’s *dharmakāya*; this [latter] reveals the elimination of even non-marks to engage with the conventional world while remaining free from false conceptualization.
It is by virtue of this principle that the two perfections differ.

Within the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), this is also first explained in general. Regarding "the emptiness of sentient beings," this refers to the emptiness of the person (*pudgala-śūnyatā*), which is a conventional designation.

Regarding "the emptiness of selflessness" (*anātma-śūnyatā*), this refers to the emptiness of the phenomena of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha-dharma-śūnyatā*); because even the phenomena that are without self are empty of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-śūnya*), these two types of emptiness are equal and without distinction.

As for the statement that the contemplation of the emptiness of the person universally dispels the nature of self and other, as well as intimacy and distance, it is therefore called "equal. This contemplation of the emptiness of phenomena pervades...

Because it dispels the characteristics of internal and external distinctions, it is said to be "without distinction. "Single contemplation" means observing with equanimity; "single unified appearance" means having no separate views.
The aforementioned term "entry" refers to entering all at once and simultaneously into the contemplation of the two emptinesses of persons and phenomena, both internally and externally.
This is called the third contemplation, the Contemplation of Equal Emptiness, which serves as the skillful means for the three moments of the Path of Vision (*darśanamārga*). That is to say:
The wisdom that internally dispels the provisional conditions of sentient beings takes the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) as its skillful means.
The wisdom that internally dispels the provisional conditions of all phenomena (*dharma*) takes the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*) of the ten practices (*caryā*) as its skillful means.

The wisdom that universally dispels the provisional conditions of all sentient beings and all phenomena takes the contemplation of universal equality and emptiness (*samatā-śūnyatā*) of the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*) as its skillful means. From these skillful means...
Because he establishes those three minds, he studies from one hundred million billion up to the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

As for "reversing the sequence," it means increasing the previous eighty-four thousand dharma-gates up to one hundred million billion dharma-gates, thereby reversing the prior contemplation of emptiness.
"Subsequent to the contemplation of emptiness, they progress successively without separation.

This means that while the preceding mind contemplates all objects as being "mind-only," the subsequent mind likewise contemplates all objects as being mind-only. "The clarity and clarity lead to quiescence":

the former clarifies the non-apprehension of the characteristics of arising, while the latter clarifies the further elimination of the characteristics of agitation. Thus, the clarity of the mind increases.

Because one cultivates the method of true illumination and contemplation of the higher stages (*bhūmi*), it is called "nurturing" (*āpyāyana*). Since it is the method of illumination and contemplation of the higher stages, one turns the cause toward the fruit.

Here, "cause" refers to the preparatory practices (*prayoga*) prior to the stages; "fruit" refers to the correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) of the stages themselves, as well as all the merits up to the stage of Buddhahood.
It is precisely by this meaning that it is termed "dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*). Furthermore, "by means of immeasurable minds" means:

The four immeasurable minds lead to rebirth within the three realms; therefore, it is said that they are not abandoned. Yet, because there is no grasping or attachment, it is said that they are not accepted.
Thus, the phrase "the Dharma of the Ten Dedications is such" serves as the summary.
The second section below explains this specifically: "Constantly employing a signless mind" means being free from the mark of sentient beings (*sattva-nimitta*).

"Constantly traversing the six realms" means the sense of rescuing and protecting sentient beings. "Contemplating that all phenomena consist merely of sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth" explains the meaning of being indestructible;
for one does not dwell upon increasing conventional designations (*prajñapti*). "Merely consisting of sensation" refers to the contemplation of the conventionality of sensation. Merely...

That which is "useful" refers to the contemplation of the conventional nature of phenomena (*dharma-prajñapti*). That which is "merely a name" refers to the contemplation of the conventional nature of names (*nāma-prajñapti*).

These are the meanings of the three types of conventional designations (*tri-prajñapti*), which shall be explained in the subsequent text. "Practicing at all times the Dharma of all Buddhas of the three periods" means following the teachings to reach everywhere;
thus it is called "equal practice. This explains the meaning of "equal to all Buddhas. "Entering the lands of all Buddhas" means arriving at the One [Vehicle].

It is the meaning of being present in all places. To bestow the Three Jewels of the Permanently Abiding upon others means that within the single mind one harbors the virtues of the Three Jewels, constantly bestowing them upon others without exhaustion; this is the meaning of the inexhaustible treasury of merit.

As for "virtue with marks," it refers to conduct that engages with phenomena and transforms sentient beings. "Uncontaminated virtue" refers to the realization that contemplates emptiness while forgetting marks. Realization...
At that time, one does not destroy conventional designations; while practicing, one does not lose the understanding of emptiness.

Because such practice and cultivation are not in mutual contradiction, it is said that they "accord with the roots of goodness of equality. As for "all phenomena," there are distinctions among the truths; as for "the aspect of a unified whole":
The signless is equality; equality is suchness (*tathatā*); therefore, it is called the "mark of suchness. That all phenomena are non-dual means not clinging to the object grasped.
That Prajñā is unborn means not clinging to the subject that grasps. Not clinging to either subject or object is the meaning of being unbound.
The equality of existence and non-existence, and the single integration of the three times, is the meaning of liberation. To awaken to all phenomena—
"The ultimate truth" explains the meaning of the *dharmadhātu*. "The Middle Way is signless;

all phenomena are uniformly characterized by illumination" explains the immeasurable meanings [of the stages] from below the thirty minds. This is the second summary of the three stages of the *śaikṣas* (the three levels of worthiness).
Below this is the second section, which explains the twelve stages (*bhūmi*). It contains two parts: a general clarification and a detailed explanation. Regarding the first part, the text says:

"As for what you previously asked, 'What is meant by "stage"?'—this was an initial general inquiry into the meaning and characteristics of the name; now, within that context, we are specifically citing the stages.
As for "that which sustains all meritorious qualities," it means that the essence of the *dharmadhātu* universally sustains and maintains all meritorious qualities.
It is just as the great earth supports mountains, seas, and so forth. Regarding its capacity to produce all causes and effects:

it can generate all virtuous causes and bring all virtuous fruits to maturity. Just as the great earth can produce sprouts and the like, and bring flowers and fruits to completion, it is for these two reasons that it is called "earth" (bhūmi).

Below this, the first stage (*bhūmi*) is explained in detail. Regarding the statement "abandoning the practices of ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana-caryā*): because one has attained the noble dharmas (*āryadharma*), one abandons the nature of an ordinary being.
"Abandoning" here carries the meaning of transcending the state of an ordinary being. The following ten phrases clarify this meaning of transcendence: First is the transcendence of lineage (*kula*).
As the sūtra says, "born into the family of the Buddhas," for the pure dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) constitutes the family of the Buddhas. Second is the transcendence of status (*avasthā*).
First, it is because of succeeding to the rank of a bodhisattva, as the sūtra says: "Because the mind of non-attainment constitutes the rank of a bodhisattva.

Second, it is because of entering the assembly of the noble ones, as the sūtra says: "Because one has entered among the ranks of the great bodhisattvas. Third, it is the transcendence of faults regarding the noble assembly.

Fourth, it is the freedom from the fault of deviance, as the sūtra says: "Because the four māras do not reach them, and the various māras and their evil obstructions cannot destroy them. Fifth, it is correct contemplation.

1. The transcendence of duality: as the sūtra states, because it equally illuminates both sides without falling into the two extremes; because it fuses existence and non-existence while simultaneously illuminating both. 2. The transcendence of superior progress:
as the sūtra states, because one’s great faith has just become full, and one practices and studies the contemplation of the Middle Way and the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of non-arising;

because one learns through faith the contemplation of the Middle Way within the Buddha-ground. 3. The transcendence of simultaneous illumination: as the sūtra states, because one constantly reaches both...
Because it encompasses the third stage through to the eleventh stage; and because it simultaneously illuminates the remaining gateways of the dharma-realm, such as the most excellent [stages].
Eighth is the transcendence of its own level: as the sūtra says, "The mind and mental factors are quiescent within the flow of the dharma-water, being of one mark and markless";
for throughout the pervasive dharma-realm, the mind and mental factors flow constantly. Ninth is the transcendence of the dharma-body: as the sūtra says, "The two bodies have no fixed location."

Therefore, tenth is the "Excellence of Buddha-fields. As the sutra states, because it universally shares in the same Buddha-fields, one rejoices in all respects based on these ten kinds of sublime merits;
thus, it is named the Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi).

Regarding "by means of the correct signlessness": one is fully endowed with right precepts and remains far removed from what is deviant and incorrect, because one does not grasp at the signs of the precepts, their observance, or their violation.

Regarding "skillfully entering the realm of sentient beings and manifesting ten thousand Buddha-worlds": this is because one accords with the natures of sentient beings while manifesting all Buddha-lands.
Regarding "the transformations of the six supernormal powers being empty and identical to the unconditioned": although there is nothing to be done, there is nothing that is not done.

Therefore, internally one abandons the turbidity of the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala*), and externally one is free from the defilement of the two extremes (*antadvaya*). For this reason, it is called the Ground of Freedom from Defilement (*vimalā-bhūmi*).

Regarding "Luminous Wisdom and Receptive Patience" (*prabhākari-adhimukti-kṣānti*): in this third ground, the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) is predominant; among the three grades of receptive patience, it occupies the highest level.
Therefore, by relying upon the twelvefold light of the Tathāgata, it illuminates the twelvefold faculties of all sentient beings;
as these lights interact and transform with one another, it is called the Stage of Radiance (Prabhākari-bhūmi).
Regarding "the patience of great conformity to non-arising": because it is the initial entry into the lower grade among the three grades of conforming patience (*anulomikī kṣānti*).

Regarding "contemplating the characteristics of the two truths of all phenomena": although this is the patience of great conformity to non-arising, one constantly observes the characteristics of existence and non-existence.

The upper contemplation is for propagating the Buddha-way above; the lower contemplation is for transforming sentient beings below. These are the third contemplations: loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity.
Adding these three to the previous four makes seven. Because the seven contemplations shine forth brilliantly, it is named the Stage of Flames (Arciṣmatī-bhūmi).
Regarding those who cultivate the path through compliant patience (*ānulomikī-kṣānti*): because they cultivate the middle grade among the three types of compliant patience.

Regarding the fact that all ignorance, doubt, and views within the three realms are entirely empty: because, by relying on the contemplation of the various truths (*satya*), they are able to overcome the afflictions (*kleśa*).

Regarding the eight analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*) as merit for entering the five sciences (*pañca-vidyā-sthāna*): because these eight and five arts surpass all worldly things. That is to say, the four analytical knowledges of cause and effect.
Regarding the distinction between the inner and outer paths, this reveals eight forms of eloquence (*pratibhāna*), as there are four each concerning cause and fruit.
Because these eight forms of eloquence are superior to those of the inner and outer paths, the four within the cause exist because there are four forms of eloquence based on the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*.

The four within the fruit exist because there are likewise four based on the *Tathāgatabhūmi*. As the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states: "Furthermore, regarding the non-obstruction of phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*)..."
Wisdom: knowing the wisdom that enters into accordance with all bodhisattva practices, dharma-practices, and wisdom-practices;

through the unimpeded wisdom of meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), knowing the entry into the distinctions of the meanings of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) as they are analytically explained; through the unimpeded wisdom of expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), explaining without impairment the paths of the various stages in accordance with them;
and through the unimpeded wisdom of eloquence (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*), explaining the immeasurable characteristics of each individual stage. The commentary says: herein...

The characteristics of the Bodhisattva stages are fourfold: first, the characteristic of wisdom; second, the characteristic of teaching; third, the characteristic of skillful means; and fourth, the characteristic of entering the immeasurable gates.
