Because these are the essence, all practices of Bodhisattvas—namely, the practice of Dharma and the practice of wisdom—are manifested through the teaching of realized knowledge.
Regarding the distinctions of the ten stages, it should be understood that "mind" refers to the teacher and "teaching" refers to verbal expression; this is the teaching of the indestructible.
Because they provide non-erroneous instruction to those who follow the stages of the path. What are the characteristics of the Tathāgata stage? The Sūtra says:
Furthermore, by means of the unimpeded knowledge of phenomena (*dharmapratisaṃvid*), one knows that all Buddhas attain perfect enlightenment in a single thought-moment.

By means of the unimpeded knowledge of meaning (*arthapratisaṃvid*), one knows the distinctions between the various characteristics of phenomena and events. By means of the unimpeded knowledge of expression (*niruktipratisaṃvid*), one explains according to the distinctions of the Perfectly Awakened One.
By means of the unimpeded knowledge of eloquence (*pratibhānapratisaṃvid*), one may explain each and every phrase of the Dharma for immeasurable eons without ever reaching exhaustion.
The commentary states: Regarding the characteristics of the stage of the Tathāgata herein, there are four kinds. The first is the characteristic of the *dharmakāya*.

Second, the marks of the form body (*rūpakāya*); third, the marks of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*); fourth, the marks of teaching. Regarding these, "time" refers to which Buddha one becomes in whichever eon.
"Activity" refers to by means of which buddha-field and according to which buddha-body. "Marks" refers to the fact that they can be seen and heard according to what is recorded by their names.
Regarding "according to perfect enlightenment," one should explain based on the ten kinds of Buddhas as taught in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Because of this knowledge. Thus, each of these two gates has four types of eloquence; therefore, they are called the eightfold merit of eloquence (*aṣṭapratibhāna-guṇa*).

"Internal and external" refers to inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*) and outer science (*bāhya-vidyā*). "Methods and paths" refers to medical arts (*cikitsā-vidyā*). "Cause and effect" refers to logic (*hetu-vidyā*), because the name of the school [of logic] is derived from its result.
"Masters of spirits" refers to various incantations and curses; this is the science of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*). By means of these, one is able to excel in the world.
In summary, all these paths are called "Difficult to Conquer" (Sudurjaya) because, internally, they conquer all afflictions, and externally, they conquer all worldly things;
they cannot be conquered by those [afflictions and worldly things], and are thus named "Difficult to Conquer."

Regarding "superiorly conforming to the contemplation of all dharmas": because it is the superior grade of conforming patience (*anulomikī-kṣānti*), the three periods of time are unified as one in tranquil illumination without duality;
since this contemplation is actively manifest, it is called the Stage of Presence (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*).
Regarding the "contemplation of the non-arising of all phenomena" among the three types of patience regarding non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*):
because one has just entered the lowest grade [of this stage], one is neither said to possess afflictions (*kleśa*) nor to be free from afflictions. As the *Daśabhūmika Sūtra* states:
"Abiding in this Bodhisattva stage of Dūraṃgamā (Far-Reaching), one is not called 'possessing afflictions,' nor is one called 'free from afflictions. Why? Because no afflictions manifest."

Therefore, because the seeking of the Tathāgata’s wisdom is not yet fulfilled, the phrase "one birth, one extinction, one fruit, the final body of the triple realm" clarifies that [the practitioner] has reached the ultimate limit of the stage of fragmented existence (*bhavāgra*).

The phrase "one entry and one exit, accumulating immeasurable merit until reaching quiescence" clarifies the long-term practice of entering meditative contemplation. It is by virtue of these two meanings that [this is so].
It is called "Far-Reaching.
As for the phrase "for this reason," it is because one has already received the final body in the preceding stages; thus, in this eighth stage, one abandons the retribution of the three realms.
Since one has abandoned the segmented [birth] within the three realms, it is said to be the function of the fruit of transformation. This belongs among the three kinds of mind-made bodies.

The Bodhisattva Mahāsthāmaprāpta possesses a mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*). One who enters the wisdom of signlessness (*animitta-prajñā*) within the stage of "intermediate patience" (*madhyama-kṣānti*) does so because they have begun to abide in the middle grade among the three grades of the patience of non-arising (*anutpatti-kṣānti*).

Regarding the phrase "emerging from existence and entering non-existence while manifesting impermanence": they constantly emerge from the truth of existence (*satya*) and perpetually enter the truth of non-existence (*asatya*).

They spontaneously observe both simultaneously, exercising mastery over manifestations, all of which are impermanent. This is based on the fact that there is no difference between emerging and entering.
The meaning of this is used to explain "immovability. As stated in the *Rājanirdeśa-sūtra* regarding the eighth stage (*bhūmi*): "While abiding in existence, one constantly cultivates emptiness;

while dwelling in emptiness, one constantly manifests myriad transformations. Thus, when one sees for oneself that the Buddhas of the future fruit will bestow empowerment by touching the crown of one's head and preach the Dharma, this refers to the future fruit accomplished through the continuity of one's own body.
Within the two types of *dharmakāya*, the ultimate *dharmakāya* is non-dual and without distinction.

The transformation bodies and dharma-bodies manifest in great numbers according to conditions. Because the bodhisattva perceives these transformation and dharma-bodies for himself, he refers to them as "all Buddhas.
Now, because this bodhisattva manifests in numerous bodies within the assemblies of all these Buddhas, each of those Buddhas preaches the Dharma for him individually.
The mind of this Bodhisattva pervades all those bodies; according to what they hear of the Dharma being taught, each practices individually.
Therefore, it is said that body and mind act separately. Such a principle is not within the realm of discursive thought; therefore, it is called "inconceivable.
This is an explanation of "immovability" based on the meaning of the certainty of the future fruit. By virtue of these two meanings, it is named the Immovable Ground (*acalā-bhūmi*).

Furthermore, regarding "again entering the superior contemplation of the radiant transformations of the Buddha": within the three patiences of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), one again enters the superior grade.
This is because there is no radiance of contemplative wisdom or radiance of physical color that is not sublime. For these two reasons, it is named the Stage of Sublime Wisdom (*sādhumatī-bhūmi*).
When the Bodhisattva at that time enters the contemplation of the Middle Way, the Supreme Truth (*paramārtha-satya*), this clarifies the ability to enter the tenth Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
This is the general statement; the following provides the specific meanings, demonstrated through ten points. First is entry by practice (*caryā-praveśa*):

as the sutra says, "practicing within the lower grade of great tranquil patience," because one practices the sphere of the Buddha’s conduct. Second is entry by reception (*pratigraha-praveśa*): as the sutra says, "sitting upon a thousand-jeweled [throne]."

1. Entry by Sign (*nimitta-praveśa*): Because one receives the Buddha’s prediction of the stage [of Buddhahood]. 2. Entry by Practice (*prayoga-praveśa*): As the sutra says, because one studies the Buddha’s transformative merit. 3. Entry by Learning (*śikṣā-praveśa*):

As the sutra says, because one studies the Buddha’s transformative merit. 4. Entry by Severance (*prahāṇa-praveśa*): As the sutra says, because the two habits (*vāsanā*) are suppressed and severed. 5. Entry by Faith (*adhimukti-praveśa*): One looks up to and believes in the Buddha’s wisdom.

As the sutra says, because great faith is accomplished. 6. Entry by Realization (*sākṣātkriyā-praveśa*): One penetrates one’s own objective realm. As the sutra says, it is equal to the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Therefore, "sameness" (*samatā*) refers to being free from the two types of discrimination—the subject and the object. "Equality" (*samatva*) refers to the state of equality throughout the three periods of time.
As the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states: "Although wisdom arises and ceases, it is because it is capable of being without arising and without cessation.

Seventh is "entry into equality," which, by relying on internally realized wisdom, achieves the quality of a single flavor. As the sūtra says regarding the two truths having a single characteristic: all meritorious qualities [are of one taste].

Therefore, the eighth is the entrance of differentiation, because through the wisdom that transforms others, one skillfully masters their faculties and capacities, as the sūtra says, "entering the faculties of sentient beings.
The ninth is the entrance of internal teaching, as the sūtra says, "immeasurable merits of necklaces. The tenth is the entrance of external form.

As it is said in the Sūtra, because it manifests all forms and characteristics at one and the same time, and because it moistens the roots of goodness of sentient beings in the six realms of existence by means of these ten kinds of meritorious dharmas,
it is called the Ground of the Dharma-Cloud (Dharmameghā-bhūmi).
Within the Stainless Ground (*vimalā-bhūmi*), there are three sections: first, the manifestation of virtues; second, the designation of the person; and third, the explanation of the ground’s name.

Regarding the first, the statement "dwelling in the gate of great tranquility, observing the middle grade of patience" means that within the fifth [ground], Great Tranquil Patience, which has three grades, one now dwells in the middle grade at this stage; this is the general statement. This dwelling consists of ten kinds. First:
First is the dwelling of fulfillment; because the causal practices are perfected, as the sūtra says, "the meritorious practices are fulfilled. Second is the dwelling of ascending;

because one ascends to the summit of the Middle Way, as the sūtra says, "ascending the great mountain terrace. Third is the dwelling of mind; because one enters hundreds of thousands of samādhis, as the sūtra says.

Fourth is the dwelling of body; because one gathers the ritual applications of the Buddhas, as the sūtra says. Fifth is the dwelling of the conditioned; because there is the ripening consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*).

The first is the dwelling of the arising and ceasing of the truth of suffering. As the sūtra says: "There are only the fruits of conditioning, which are impermanent and subject to arising and ceasing.

The sixth is the dwelling of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), which is far removed from all conceptualization and volitional activity. As the sūtra says: "The mind and mental factors are unconditioned. The seventh is the dwelling that transcends the lower realms.

In the ten lower stages (*bhūmi*), the causal practices are not yet fulfilled, as the *sūtra* states that one must pass beyond these ten stages. Eighth is the dwelling of the same as above: illuminating the summit of the Middle Way;
the Buddha-wisdom is not surpassed, as the *sūtra* states that one’s understanding is identical to that of a Buddha. Ninth is the dwelling of the place of sitting:

constantly sitting upon the Tathāgata’s seat to preach the Dharma for sentient beings, as the *sūtra* states that one sits in the place where the Buddha sits. Tenth is the dwelling of the objective realm.
Regarding the two truths as all phenomena: there is no phenomenon that the two types of wisdom do not perceive. As the Sūtra states:
"Because their wisdom perceives the objects of all phenomena, both the permanent and the impermanent. To say "perceives the two" means that they have not yet transcended the two truths.

One should know that the names are established by defining them through mutual contrast. Within this, there are two parts: first, the establishment [of the names], and second, the explanation. The section beginning with "The reason why... constitutes the second part, the explanation.
"Great power of transformation" refers to the power of supernatural penetrations (*abhijñā*). "A hundred kalpas or ten thousand kalpas" is a concise way of referring to a thousand kalpas.

Regarding the "eightfold wheel of Dharma," for those of the two vehicles, one turns the wheel of the four noble truths with conditioned activity (*saṃskṛta*); for Bodhisattvas, one turns the wheel of the four noble truths without conditioned activity (*asaṃskṛta*).
As for the statement that "all dharmas, whether advancing or halting, are identical," it is by virtue of this meaning that one is said to be "training in the Buddha-way."
The following provides the formal explanation of the names of the stages (*bhūmi*). The term "this" refers back to what was previously stated.
Regarding "entering the Vajra-samādhi": based on the hundreds of thousands of samādhis by which one has previously dwelt, one enters the final Vajra-samādhi.
At this time, because one is not destroyed by various marks (*nimitta*), it is said to be "one mark, which is markless. Furthermore, one is also not obstructed by any defilements.
Therefore, it is said to be "quiescent and unconditioned. For this reason, it is called the "Stainless Ground" (*vimalā-bhūmi*).

Within the "Ground of Sublime Enlightenment" (*sudarśana-bhūmi*), there are also three parts: the general heading, the detailed explanation, and the third, the concluding summary. Regarding the initial general heading, which states:
"The sublime enlightenment, superior patience, great quiescence, and signless contemplation": among the three grades of great quiescent patience, sublime enlightenment is at the highest level.

Because this is the specific analysis, there are two phrases within it. The first phrase reveals the virtues; the second phrase explains the name. Within the revelation of virtues, there are two sub-phrases:
the first reveals the pervasiveness of the merit of benefiting others, and the latter reveals the perfection of the merit of self-benefit.
The phrase "only by means of the wholesome dharmas arising from the conditions of all sentient beings" indicates that the Tathāgata’s perfect wisdom is effortless (*anābhoga*).
The mind, by means of the capacities and conditions of all sentient beings, spontaneously and universally gives rise to all wholesome dharmas;
this is the perfection of the merit of benefiting others. Furthermore, as for one who personally maintains all merits:
although they constantly bestow all wholesome dharmas upon others, they never lose their own internal, perfect virtues; this is the perfection of the merit of self-benefit. By means of these two—

Because it signifies the ultimate meaning, it is called the "Buddha-treasury. Below this is the second section, which explains the term "Sublime Enlightenment" (Miaojue). This section consists of two parts: the formal explanation and the differentiation.

Regarding the phrase "tranquilly illuminating all phenomena": although there is no deliberate effort (*anābhoga*), there is universal illumination. "Tranquility" (*jì*) is the sense of "sublime" (*miào*).

Because it is far removed from the disturbances of arising, ceasing, and activation; "illumination" (*zhào*) has the meaning of awakening, as it eternally severs the slumber of the darkness of ignorance.
For these two reasons, it is called "Wondrous Awakening" (*miaojue*). To distinguish this from what follows:

all Bodhisattvas from the stage of Buddhahood downward who possess "illumination and quiescence" (*zhaoji*) merely illuminate the principle of original quiescence and extinction; therefore, they are called "illumination and quiescence. However, within their [state]...

The mind has not yet departed from arising and ceasing; thus, the wisdom that can illuminate is not free from ignorance. For this reason, it is unable to achieve quiescent illumination and is not termed "wondrous enlightenment.
Within the third section, which provides a general conclusion, there are two parts: first, pointing to the detailed explanation; second, concluding the brief explanation.

In the "Chapter on the Mother of the Buddhas" (*Buddhamātṛ-parivarta*), based on the extensive opening section that reveals the core tenets of the sutra, the four chapters are divided into two parts. The preceding section has completed the formal exposition of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
The following chapter reveals the realm of the six sense bases. Regarding the term "Mother of the Buddhas": the mother is that which gives birth and nurtures.
The meaning of this is that the *sarvākārajñatā* (all-aspect wisdom) of all Buddhas of the three periods of time arises based upon the Middle Way of the two truths;
since this point clearly elucidates that meaning, it is therefore named the "Chapter on the Mother of the Buddhas."

The section beginning with "At that time" contains two parts in the text: first, the explicit elucidation of the Mother of Buddhas; second, the analysis through various categories. Within the first part, there are also two sections:
first, the question; second, the answer. In the question, there are two sub-sections: first, the question regarding wisdom; second, the question regarding the object.
At the beginning, two things are mentioned. First, regarding the "wisdom that illuminates": this refers to the initial wisdom of the Buddha and the initial wisdom of the Bodhisattva;

it is the initial wisdom that is cited because it gives rise to the inquiry into the meaning [of reality]. Furthermore, as for the meaning of "tranquil illumination" (*jizhao*) and "illumination of tranquility" (*zhaoji*): upon what does the wisdom of tranquil illumination depend for its arising?
This is a general inquiry concerning both the initial and final wisdoms. Within the inquiry regarding the objects, there are also two parts:

first, an inquiry into the *dharmatā* of the two truths; second, an inquiry into the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). In the response, the two preceding questions are answered in succession. Regarding the first question, the direct answer provides a further explanation.
This direct answer consists of two parts: first, it clarifies that the three truths serve as the "mother"; second, it reveals that the various gates [of teaching] serve as the "mother. It says:
"Up to and including" (*yāvat*) refers to the following: among the sixteen truths, three truths are first presented, after which the thirteen gates of truth are revealed.

This is because there is not a single dharma-gate that does not serve as the mother of wisdom. The section beginning with the "two truths" below answers the subsequent question; it consists of three parts in the text:

the restatement (*uddeśa*), the explanation (*nirdeśa*), and the conclusion (*upasaṃhāra*). Within the explanation, there are two parts: the specific explanation and the general clarification. The specific explanation of the two truths is as follows:

There are four gates: first, the gate of existence and non-existence; second, the gate of duality and non-duality; third, the gate of causes and conditions; fourth, the gate of provisional names. Regarding the gate of existence and non-existence:

it refers to the nature of conceptualization (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), which possesses both principle and phenomena. In terms of principle, they are provisionally existent, and this provisional existence is not empty;

this is called the Truth of Existence (*astitva-satya*). In terms of phenomena, they are truly non-existent, and this true non-existence is emptiness; this is called the Truth of Non-existence (*nāstitva-satya*). As the Sūtra says:

Because conventional truth exists, it is not empty; because ultimate truth is empty, it does not exist. Thus, these two truths are always such and never otherwise, and for this reason they are not one.
Yet, since in reality they are not so [in a dualistic sense], they are not two. As the Sūtra says: "The two truths are always thus, and therefore they are not one."

Because the noble ones perceive emptiness, there is non-duality. Within this, the two truths are eternally as they are: because conventional existence cannot be established as conventional existence, and ultimate non-existence cannot be established as ultimate existence;
this is what is differentiated by the wisdom that accords with phenomena (*yathābhūta-jñāna*). As for the noble ones perceiving emptiness:

because conventional existence cannot be established as conventional existence, and ultimate non-existence cannot be established as ultimate non-existence; this is what is realized by the wisdom that accords with reality (*yathāvad-jñāna*).
As for why "provisional existence" cannot be established as provisional existence: it is provisionally established based on names;

however, because the names upon which it depends cannot be apprehended, the dependent provisional existence cannot be established. As for why "actual non-existence" cannot be established as actual non-existence:

one establishes actual non-existence by negating the imagined existence; however, because the actual existence that is to be negated cannot be apprehended, the negation itself [cannot be established].
In reality, there is nothing that cannot be established. Because the wisdom of suchness penetrates in this manner, it is said that the noble illumination of emptiness is non-dual.
This constitutes the first gate, the principle of the two truths. Herein, non-duality correctly manifests true suchness;
this is precisely the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya). Regarding the second gate, that of duality and non-duality: as previously stated, there is one truth...
That which is without differentiation, eternally thus, and unchanging is called the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

That in which both existence and non-existence are empty and equal in a single flavor is therefore called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). As the sutra says: "Whether a Buddha appears or not, the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is unchanging;

therefore it is not empty. Because it is the foremost and non-dual, it is not existent. Herein, the "dharma-realm" is conventionally existent but ultimately non-existent, its boundaries remaining undisturbed.
Therefore, it is called the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). When a Buddha appears in the world, he speaks of the realm of existence and non-existence;

after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, this realm of existence and non-existence remains unchanged. For this reason, one first says "there is a Buddha" and later says "there is no Buddha. This is the first non-duality.

Because this ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is without dual characteristics; and because there is thus a distinction between existence and non-existence in conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), it is not identical with the ultimate truth.
Because existence and non-existence are not established, it is not different from the ultimate truth. As the Sūtra says:

"Because the Buddha and the Buddha-dharma within the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) have two distinct characteristics, they are not one; because all phenomena are eternally pure, they are not two. Thus, the Buddha...

When a Buddha appears in the world, the boundaries between existence and non-existence remain undisturbed. When a Buddha appears in the world, existence and non-existence are as they were originally, without confusion;
this is because the Buddha’s appearance does not arise from the illumination of duality. It is the conceptual boundaries of existence and non-existence that give rise to differentiation.
Therefore, it is first said that there is no Buddha, and subsequently that there is a Buddha. To say that all phenomena are eternally pure means that they accord with words.
All marks are unestablished; therefore, they are non-dual with the markless. Third is the gate of the two truths regarding causes and conditions:
although the Buddhas have already transcended the three realms and all conditioned activities, they enter the six paths in response to karmic conditions.

Through such a gathering of responsive causes and conditions, one knows that what is not non-existent is called the truth of existence (*satya*). Although it is not non-existent, it cannot be [grasped as] existent.
There is existence. Because it cannot be grasped as existing, it is provisionally called non-existence. Although it is called non-existence, non-existence itself does not persist.
When both existence and non-existence are absent, this is termed the Truth of Non-existence (*asatya*). As the sutras state: "The Buddhas, for the sake of ordinary beings, do not [assert] emptiness;

because there is no non-existence, they do not [assert] existence. As stated above in the text: "Because of the gathering of causes and conditions, it is called existence; it is not that 'existence' is inherently existent. Because of causes and conditions..."
Because it is dispersed, it is called "non-existent. This does not mean that there is such a thing as a "non-existence"; rather, this precisely refers to the two truths within this gate.
The *Rājanirdeśa-sūtra* states: "Non-existence is non-existent even in truth; quiescent cessation is the supreme emptiness. All phenomena exist through causes and conditions;
such is the meaning of existence and non-existence. In this context, because the emptiness of the truth of non-existence is ultimate reality, it is not identical with the truth of existence.
Because the dharma of existence is fundamentally unarisen, it does not constitute a duality with the truth of non-existence;

therefore, it is said that because emptiness is real, they are not one. Because the primordial limit is unarisen, they are not two. This gate of the two truths is itself the Middle Way, the primary meaning.
Why is this so? Because existence is unarisen, it is the truth of non-existence; because non-existence is also empty, it is the truth of existence. Thus...
The two truths are themselves the Middle Way, as stated above: "Because the two truths and the one truth are of a single unified character.

Regarding the fourth gate, the provisional designation of the two truths: the collection of the three types of provisional designations is called the worldly truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), while the true reality (*dharmatā*) is called the truth of ultimate meaning (*paramārtha-satya*).
As the Sūtra says, because it does not destroy the provisional designations of the characteristics of all phenomena, they are not empty; yet these phenomena are not [ultimately] phenomena.

Therefore, because they do not exist as such. The *Puruṣarāja-sūtra* states: "The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally without nature; it is the suchness of the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).

All that exists is fundamentally a phenomenon of existence, a conventional existence formed by the collection of the three types of designation (*tri-prajñapti*). This precisely refers to the characteristics of the two truths within this gateway. As for the "three designations": [they are]...

That which is called the conventionality of phenomena (*dharma-prajñapti*), the conventionality of experience (*anubhava-prajñapti*), and the conventionality of names (*nāma-prajñapti*): herein, the conventionality of names is the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), because it is by relying on the conventionality of names that the characteristics of all phenomena are established.
The two conventions of experience and phenomena are the nature of dependence on others (*paratantra-svabhāva*), because they resemble persons and resemble phenomena, yet are neither real.
These three conventional dharmas are not [ultimate] dharmas; therefore, they do not constitute a duality with the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).

Although they are not dharmas, they are not non-dharmas either; therefore, they do not constitute a unity with the ultimate truth. Thus it is said that because they are both dharmas and non-dharmas, they are not two;
and because they are not non-dharmas, they are not one. The detailed explanation of the two truths has already been concluded above.
Below this, the second section provides a general explanation of the "Eight Negations" (*aṣṭāvinaya*). In interpreting the meaning of this passage, there are briefly two approaches:

first, the general approach; second, the specific approach. Regarding the general approach: as previously stated, within each of the four gates of the two truths (*satyadvaya*), there are these four pairs of eight negations.
What is the meaning of this? This first pair—neither one nor two—generally explains all four gates.

"Neither one nor two": because the words and their meaning are no different from what preceded, this second pair—neither eternal nor annihilated—universally explains the four gates of neither empty nor existent.
For existence constitutes eternity, while non-existence leads to annihilation.
"Neither coming nor going" further clarifies the initial pair of neither one nor two; for emptiness and existence are not one, and existence does not [arise] from...
It comes from emptiness, because emptiness and existence are non-dual; thus, emptiness does not drive existence away.

Regarding the fourth [characteristic], "neither arising nor ceasing," this further clarifies the second [characteristic], "neither eternal nor annihilated. Because there is no arising, it is not existent; because there is no ceasing, it is not non-existent.
Non-existence has the meaning of annihilation, and existence is the extreme of eternalism. Therefore, these eight [characteristics] do not apply to the four gates. If one proceeds...
Another interpretation explains the sequential manifestation of these four pairs. Regarding those first four gates, what is their meaning?
Herein, "neither one nor two" reveals that the first pair of the two truths is free from extremes;

for they are not one because [the conventional] exists and is impermanent, and they are not two because noble wisdom illuminates emptiness. Second, "neither eternal nor annihilated" reveals the second...
The second gate is the Middle Way of the two truths, which is free from extremes: because the dharma-realm is unchanging, it is not annihilated;
because it is primordially non-dual, it is not eternal. Regarding the third, "neither coming nor going," this reveals the middle way of the two truths within the third gate:

because phenomena arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions, they have no point of origin; because causes and conditions disperse, they have no destination. Fourth, "neither arising... [and so forth].
"Non-extinction" reveals the Middle Way of the two truths within the fourth section. Because it does not destroy conventional designations, it is not subject to arising;
because it employs the manifestation of the true nature (*dharmatā*), it is not subject to extinction. This is called the meaning of the eight negations according to the distinct sections.
As for "the two aspects being identical and the noble wisdom being non-dual," since the four pairs previously discussed are all inseparable, one is free from all extremes and thus...
Regarding "conformity": it means that non-identity is itself non-duality, and so on, up to non-extinction being itself non-arising.

In this way, such characteristics are far removed from all extremes. Likewise, the characteristics of these two truths are inseparable. Therefore, the two types of wisdom conform to their objects without duality;
thus, the non-dual realm of the two truths can serve as the mother of the non-dual two wisdoms. For this reason...
Because it is non-dual, it is the mother of the wisdom of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Briefly stated, there are three meanings of this "mother of wisdom.

First, it is the nature of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*) of all sentient beings, upon which initial enlightenment (*ādikṣaya-bodhi*) relies; thus, it is called the mother of wisdom, as it serves as the fundamental substance for initial enlightenment.
Second, it is that upon which the present wisdom of the future Buddha-fruition of all Bodhisattvas relies.

Therefore, it is called the Mother of Wisdom (*jñānamātṛ*). When it has not yet been attained, it is called Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*); when it has already been attained, it is called *sarvajñatā* (omniscience). As stated in the *Rājaputra-sūtra*:
"The fundamental Mother of Wisdom that is the nature of all sentient beings is itself the essence of *sarvajñatā*.

For all Buddhas of the future, the one who will become a Buddha serves as the Mother of Wisdom; when unattained, it is called 'nature,' and when attained, it is *sarvajñatā*. This applies to the three vehicles (*triyāna*) as well.
Prajñā is neither arising nor ceasing; its self-nature is eternally abiding.

Because all sentient beings take this as their awakened nature (*bodhigotra*), it is said—according to the commentary—that from the level of the three vehicles downward, the first nature of original awakening (*mūla-awakening*) is further elucidated; therefore, it is called "eternally abiding" and is also termed "awakened nature.
Third, within the Middle Way of the two truths, it is neither original nor subsequent, yet it can give rise to sagely wisdom; thus, it is named "wisdom" (*jñāna*).
"Mother. In this passage, the third meaning is revealed. The section beginning with "The ten directions" below is the third summary.
The preceding portion concludes the exposition on the Mother of Correct Wisdom.

Below this is the second section, the analysis by way of various categories (*dvāra-vibhāga*). This contains two parts: first, the questions; second, the answers. Within the initial questions, three inquiries are raised:
first, a question regarding the sudden or gradual nature of the awakening; second, a question regarding whether that which is abandoned is one or many;

third, a question regarding the duration and brevity of the number of kalpas spent in cultivation. Within the answers, there are two parts: first, praising the questions and granting permission to speak; second, responding to the questions.
The direct answer: herein, the three preceding questions are answered in sequence. First, the initial question is answered, which consists of two parts: the direct answer and the concluding summary.
Within the first part, it is clearly explained that this is sudden and not gradual. Now, regarding this distinction between the gradual and the sudden, there are two meanings:

first, the gradual and sudden according to the person; second, the gradual and sudden in relation to the object. As for the gradual and sudden according to the person, if one relies on the continuity of a single individual...
From beginning to end, one gradually purifies all outflows (*āsrava*) and one’s wisdom gradually increases.

However, if one relies on the many continuities (*saṃtati*) of various individuals, one suddenly purifies all outflows and suddenly attains perfect enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* says: "For example, the *āmra* fruit ripens gradually and not all at once.
Mahāmati, the purification of the stream of manifestations of one's own mind by sentient beings is likewise."

It is so. Purification occurs gradually, not all at once. Furthermore, Mahāmati, it is like the Ālayavijñāna, which simultaneously cognizes the manifested objects—the self-body, the means of subsistence, and the vessel-world—rather than doing so sequentially.
The *saṃbhogakāya* Tathāgata is likewise; he simultaneously brings all realms of sentient beings to fulfillment and establishes them in the ultimate, pure, and wondrous state.
"The palace is a place for practicing purity," and so forth, as explained at length. Regarding the second pair of objects, clarifying the gradual and sudden:
if one confronts the tenfold dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) to subdue and eliminate the ten kinds of obscurations and so on, one must eliminate them gradually, and thus one's wisdom increases gradually.
If, however, one confronts the single door of the dharma-realm to permanently sever the innate ignorance (upapattilābhikī avidyā), this is direct and sudden awakening; it is also termed "sudden."

It is severed. This is because from the stage of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) and below, one relies solely on faith and has not yet attained direct vision. As the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* states:
"From the stage of *śīla-kṣānti* (patience in practice) up to the *mūrdhan-samādhi* (summit concentration), all are termed 'subduing all afflictions.

Yet, while there is faith and belief, there is no extinction of all afflictions nor the arising of the wisdom of liberation that illuminates the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). Therefore, these are not termed 'vision' (*darśana*). What is meant by "vision"?

This is *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). Therefore, since ancient times, I have always taught that from the *mūrdhan-samādhi* (crown samādhi) known, seen, and realized only by the Buddha, down to the stage of *kṣānti* (patience) based on faith, there is nothing unknown, unseen, or unrealized. Only the Buddha understands it instantaneously; it is not called "faith.

As for those who subdue [the mind] gradually, although their wisdom may be extinguished, they are able to abide in non-arising and non-extinction. If this mind were to be extinguished, it would constitute a burden.
There is nothing that does not cease; there is neither arising nor ceasing, as explained at length elsewhere.
In this present passage, the meaning of "sudden" (頓) is revealed by means of two approaches.

First, the statement that one hundred and eighty million stainless bodhisattvas attained the source of the Dharma-nature while seated refers to how these individuals, by realizing the source of the One Mind in a single moment, achieved wondrous enlightenment. Next, the term "sudden" [is explained].
To realize that all phenomena are non-dual and of a single integrated nature (*ekaghanalakṣaṇa*) is to clarify sudden awakening (*tongjue*) by means of the objective realm.

This "single integrated nature" refers to the one *dharmadhātu*. The preceding two lines clarify the meaning of self-awakening (*svabodha*); from the passage beginning with "From the Dharma assembly... onwards, the meaning of awakening others (*parabodha*) is revealed.
Therefore, the second part below provides the response, which contains two sections: the summary of suddenness and the summary of sameness. First, the summary:
Within the section on sudden [awakening], there are two phrases. "There is no gradual awakening of the World-Honored One" concludes the meaning that all people attain realization simultaneously.

"Only the Tathāgata possesses sudden awakening" concludes the meaning of the sudden awakening to the unified totality (*ekaghanatva*). From "the three periods of time" onwards, it concludes the common exposition.

The following is the second response, which addresses the question of identity and difference. This section contains two parts: first, the refutation of their identity; second, the concession of their difference.
Within the first part, there are three sub-sections: first, a general refutation; second, a specific explanation of the faults [of identity]; third, citing individuals to conclude the refutation.
Regarding the initial statement "ignorance" (*avidyā*), it refers to the treasury of ignorance, namely the beginningless *avidyāvāsabhūmi* (ground of the dwelling of ignorance).
That which is called "mind" refers to the mental cognition whose nature is the self-characteristic mind. The details regarding this shall be explained in the subsequent text.
This self-characteristic mind persists until one reaches the stage of Buddhahood; its ignorance (*avidyā*) is a dharma that must be abandoned. Therefore, they cannot be considered identical.
In specifically revealing the faults, four faults are manifested: first, the fault that ordinary beings and sages would not be distinct; second, [the fault regarding] the Great...

The fault of the taste not being different [from the object]. Third, citing the correct to reveal the deviant. Fourth, using the near to illustrate the distant. Regarding the first [of these four], there are two parts:

the direct exposition and the reiterated explanation. Within the direct exposition, the term "understanding" (*jie*) refers to the spiritual understanding of the bodily form, up to the wisdom-understanding that realizes the principle.
What is called "ignorance" (avidyā) refers to fundamental ignorance (*mūla-avidyā*). What are called "various views" refer to the seven types of views and so forth.

If the awakening of the spirit were identical with ignorance, then its wisdom and understanding would be identical with the various views; thus, there would be neither bondage nor liberation, and ordinary beings and sages would be one and the same.
The commentary contains two parts: a direct explanation and an expanded explanation. Within the latter, it says, "yet they share a single mind," referring to ignorance and the various views.
"Because they share a single mind of understanding. "Arising and ceasing simultaneously" means that they do not exist sequentially but are together within a single *kṣaṇa*.

"Not distinct" concludes the preceding point regarding the single mind. "Not different" concludes the preceding point regarding the single time. The fault of the "great flavor" being non-different can be understood [from this].
"All Bodhisattvas and below" marks the third section, which raises the correct to reveal the erroneous. "Furthermore, by... marks the fourth section.

Regarding the remote circumstances of the present: as for those who hold that within the signless mind there is ignorance (*avidyā*), that master maintains that all phenomena are not fixed as either this or that.
Where there is the wholesome, there must be the unwholesome; where there is knowledge, there must be non-knowledge.

For example, in the case of a single noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*): viewed from a lower perspective, its knowing is termed "wisdom" (*prajñā*); viewed from a higher perspective, its lack of knowing is precisely "ignorance. Thus he asserts.
To hold such a position results in a great error; the phrase "and yet... marks the third point, which concludes the refutation. The section beginning with "My dharma...
constitutes the second part, which grants [the opponent's] distinction. This contains two sub-sections: first, a brief summary distinguishing right from wrong;

second, a detailed exposition of the characteristics of their difference. Within the summary of right and wrong, there are four propositions. The first proposition grants that they may be identical in practice.

The practitioner is a conventionally designated sentient being. The activity of sentient beings governs all phenomena in their entirety. The meaning of "sentient being" refers to receiving birth in various places:
vertically, they traverse the three periods of time; horizontally, they grasp the five aggregates. Because they grasp the five aggregates, [they are bound].
Both good and evil belong to a single person because they traverse the three periods of time; thus, they continue in succession through a hundred kalpas.

This is the correct principle of the Buddha-dharma. The second phrase negates the notion of a single mind; for the mind is a dharma among the aggregates (skandhas), and dharmas are characterized by differentiation.
Good and evil are not the same; what precedes and follows are not uniform. For this reason, they cannot share a single mind.
The third phrase cites the Buddha to prove their distinctness; the fourth phrase cites the fruit to challenge the notion of unity. The brief examination of right and wrong has been concluded above.

Therefore, the following section extensively elucidates the distinct characteristics [of cause and effect]. This consists of four parts: first, distinguishing between the causes and effects of good and evil;

second, further clarifying the good causes and good effects; third, harmonizing the teachings and principles so they do not contradict one another; and fourth, precisely explaining that there is no discrepancy between the effects and their causes.

Regarding the first part, the statement "all who receive the fruit of Buddhahood through goodness" refers to both innate goodness (*upapatti-lābhika-kuśala*) and cultivated goodness (*prāyogika-kuśala*).
Attaining the wholesome constitutes the direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*) for all [attainments], because it results in the fruit of Buddhahood.

Regarding the case where ignorance receives the fruit of conditioned arising and cessation, both the innate ignorance (*upapatti-labdha-avidyā*) and the acquired ignorance (*prāpti-avidyā*) constitute the direct cause, because they result in the fruit of arising and cessation.

Therefore, what follows cites the fruit to conclude the discussion of the cause. Causes and fruits that accord with principle are collectively termed "wholesome" (*kuśala*), while causes and fruits that contradict principle are collectively termed "unwholesome" (*akuśala*).
Thus, from "Therefore" onwards is the second section, which further clarifies the good causes and their good fruits. Within this, there are two phrases:

the first directly explains, and the second provides a further explanation. Regarding the first, the statement "Good does not receive the fruit of arising and ceasing" means that good is not ignorance.
It is also because it is quiescent. Those who receive only the fruit of the eternal Buddha do so because virtue is concordant with the nature of quiescence.

In the reiterated explanation, it is stated that all virtues of both ordinary beings and sages are termed "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*); this explains the reason why they receive only the eternal fruit.
Because they are concordant with the nature of quiescence and oppose all outflows (*āsrava*), they are called "outflow-free. This is why it is so.
This is due to causes and conditions. Regarding the phrase "due to causes," it means that innate goodness (*upapattilābhika-kuśala*) accords with original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya-parivṛtti*).
It proceeds directly from the intrinsically pure original enlightenment, and from this it transforms into various acquired forms of goodness (*prāyogika-kuśala*).

Therefore, all wholesome dharmas of ordinary beings accord with the quiescent nature of original enlightenment and oppose all outflows (*āsrava*); thus they are called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*). This is the analysis of the meaning.
"Manifesting and emerging to receive training" refers to the category of awakening (*bodhipakṣa*). Regarding the statement "by means of conditions":

all roots of goodness existing within the mundane world grow and flourish by relying upon the Buddhas' unconditional great compassion (*nirālamba-mahākaruṇā*) as an impartial field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).

Therefore, because it accords with the Tathāgata’s field of merit and opposes all outflows (*āsrava*), it is called "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*). Since these two conditions are by nature outflow-free, [it is not...]
Having attained this, one returns to tranquility; by returning to tranquility, one receives the fruit of eternal abiding.

As stated in the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, the Buddha said to Ānanda: "If a person, being attached to the retributive fruits of the three realms of existence, practices giving or performs other roots of goodness toward the Buddha-field, and makes the vow:
'May I not enter nirvāṇa in life after life,' then by virtue of these roots of goodness, they shall not enter nirvāṇa."
There is such a possibility. Although this person does not seek nirvāṇa with delight, they have planted various roots of goodness under the Buddha;
I declare that such a person will certainly enter nirvāṇa. According to this, "entering nirvāṇa" here refers to entering the Great Parinirvāṇa of the Tathāgata.
Because they are led by the field of merit that is the Buddha, it is identical to the fruit of the *Buddhābhigīta-sūtra* mentioned above. And as for the rest...
Regarding the statement that there are "outflow-tainted" (*sāsrava*) wholesome states, this is said from the perspective of contingent conditions; therefore, there is no contradiction.

The following section provides a third reconciliation, which first reconciles the provisional teachings and subsequently accords with the ultimate principle. Within the former, it is stated that one "receives outflow-tainted fruits."
This refers to the Sūtras, which state that the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths lead to the fruits of human and celestial rebirths.

The Tathāgata, in order to transform inferior sentient beings who fear the sufferings of the three miserable realms and seek the pleasures of humans and devas, and who turn their backs on the evil conduct of the three karmas to practice various wholesome dharmas, spoke thus with reference to the *pratyaya-hetu* (conditional cause).

As for what is called the *pratyaya-hetu*, it refers to the ten wholesome paths and so forth; if viewed in relation to the fruit of Buddhahood, these constitute the *hetu-hetu* (direct cause). Regarding...
The retributions of humans and devas serve merely as conditional causes (*pratyaya-hetu*); the cause of retribution itself is simply a dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

This is the reconciliation of the scriptural teaching. Next, regarding the principle: the statement that [these] are not causes of outflows (*āsrava*) because they are the results received through ignorance (*avidyā*), karma, and feeling (*vedanā*) means that, as previously stated, various wholesome states do not receive the fruits of outflows.
All worldly fruits of birth and cessation that involve outflows are precisely what is received through ignorance, karma, and feeling. Therefore...

Because it does not constitute the direct fruit of wholesome karma. Within this context, regarding the experience of the fruit of the karma of ignorance: through the power of ignorance, the movement of the mind is not perceived;

the characteristic of this movement of the mind is called the *karmic consciousness* (*karmavijñāna*). Ignorance and karma serve as the primary causes that universally produce all fruits of birth and death.
This is what is called the principle of cause and effect according to reality. This explains the integration of doctrine and principle.
It is concluded as follows. Below this is the fourth section, a detailed explanation of the fruit and the cause. This section has two parts: first the fruit, and later the cause.

Regarding the statement in the section on the fruit, "These are called the three feelings and the three sufferings," it means that the fruits received through the karma of ignorance are precisely the three feelings, which are also termed the three sufferings.
The feeling of suffering exists in the evil destinies; the other two exist in the good paths. Among these, there is pleasure.

The feeling of equanimity (*upekṣā-vedanā*) exists from the third dhyāna downward; the feeling of equanimity exists from the fourth dhyāna upward. Painful feeling (*duḥkha-vedanā*) is called the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*); pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*) is called the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*);
the third, the feeling of equanimity, is called the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Generally speaking, all three feelings are the suffering of conditioned formations.

This is the manifestation of the distinctions among the results. Below, the two feelings are distinguished in relation to their causes. Regarding those that take wholesome causes and effects as objects:
The results of wholesome karma are the dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*) for the two feelings of pleasure and equanimity.
The results of unwholesome karma are the cause of the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*). All these are suffering, with ignorance as their root;

that is, all three types of feeling are the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), because they equally have ignorance as their fundamental cause. Thus, there are distinctions of quality and degree between the wholesome and the unwholesome.

Because there are three grades [of karma], the fruits consist of the distinct sufferings of the three miserable realms. Because wholesome [karma] has two distinctions—coarse and refined—the fruits differ as pleasure or equanimity.

Coarse wholesome [karma] includes both the distracted and the concentrated; thus, pleasure extends through both the desire and form realms. Refined wholesome [karma] pertains to the mind of attachment.

Setting aside the realms of form and formlessness, it is thus that good and evil, light and heavy, and the refined and coarse of the three realms are all equally rooted in ignorance and the karmic consciousness (*karma-vijñāna*).
Therefore, the various sufferings of the three miserable paths and the various sensations within the three realms have momentary suffering (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) as their essence.
This is because, within the cause, there is no thickness or thinness in ignorance, nor is there coarseness or subtlety in the marks of karma; therefore, such is the nature of its fruit.

In the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*), there is no distinction between light and heavy; in each moment, there is neither leisure nor haste. Therefore, it is said that all is suffering and ignorance is its root.
One should know that the principle of cause and effect is without the slightest discrepancy.
The following is the third response to the third question. It consists of two parts: restating the question and answering the question.
Within the answer, there are also two further parts: first, clarifying the number of kalpas; second, revealing the duration of practicing the path. The first of these also has two sub-sections.
First, the measure of the three grades of kalpas is determined; subsequently, the names of the various numerous kalpas are distinguished.

Regarding the first [of these], it says "three *zhu*": six *zhu* constitute one *fen*, and thus three *zhu* is half a *fen*. Below all worthy sages (*ārya*), next the duration of practicing the Path is clarified.
Within this, there are two parts: first, the duration of the time of practice is clarified; second, the quantity of the methods of practice is revealed. Regarding the first of these, there is also...
2. The actual explanation and specific clarification.

Within the actual explanation, the phrase "all worthies and sages enter the stage of number" means that from the initial entry into the principle of number by the three types of worthies, up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment as its final limit—traversing one hundred kalpas within this interval—refers to taking the aforementioned kalpa of ten thousand *li* as a single unit, until reaching one hundred such kalpas; therefore, it is so named.
"Even for a hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas. Next, the specific distinction is made: "If one enters this number, one will attain Buddhahood before long.

This is because even though it passes through a hundred thousand [kalpas], it is not considered long; furthermore, because one attains perfect enlightenment at the very moment of first generating the mind (*prathamacittotpāda*), and because it is already known that a hundred thousand [kalpas] enter into a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*).
"If one does not enter [this state], they are not called a Bodhisattva" means that they have not yet attained non-retrogression (*avaivartika*).
Because they are not actual bodhisattvas. Regarding the "Dharma-gates," the following clarifies the extent of the practices; therein are two parts:
first, the clarification of their progressive increase, and second, the conclusion summarizing their inclusion.
○ Chapter on Cause and Effect:
Regarding the "Chapter on Cause and Effect," within the two sections taught by the Tathāgata, the first—the extensive opening of the gates—has already been concluded above.
Hereafter, secondly, the core tenets of the sutra are distinguished according to the concise summary of the gates. Within this, the two gates of cause and effect are briefly established.
This comprehensively subsumes the practices and virtues of the six stages and the forty-two noble ones (*ārya*).

That which is derived is the cause; that which arises is the fruit. Because they arise in mutual dependence, they are collectively termed cause and fruit. This chapter clarifies this meaning; therefore, it is titled the "Chapter on Cause and Fruit.

The text consists of two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. Within the question, there are two sections: the summary of what preceded and the subsequent inquiry. Within the answer, there are likewise two distinct sections.
Answer: The response consists of two parts: first the cause, and second the result. Within the section on the cause, there are also two parts:

first, clarifying that which gives rise to the root; second, manifesting the virtues produced therefrom. In the first of these, there are also two parts: a general explanation and a specific exposition.

Within the general explanation, there are three phrases. The first raises the person and indicates their practice; regarding the "ten prajñās," it means that all ten perfections take wisdom as [their essence].
Because it is the foremost. [This is] because without wisdom, one cannot abandon the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala*). Second is the explanation of the root; third is the conclusion of the root.
Within the detailed explanation, first the text is cited, and then it is explained. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states that within each of the ten perfections there are ten types.
Now, in this present sutra, three triads are established briefly to subsume those ten-tens. Among these, the first seven passages are clear and can be understood. As for the [remaining] section...

Regarding "skillfully reconciling existence and non-existence within the three states": because causes and conditions combine, it is called "existence," yet this does not mean that existence is inherently existent;

because causes and conditions disperse, it is called "non-existence," yet this does not mean that existence becomes nonexistent. If one understands it in this way, all difficult questions will be resolved without exception;
hence, it is called "skillful reconciliation. Regarding "neither abandoning nor accepting": this refers to [the attitude toward] saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
Dharmas are like dreams; they are neither existent nor non-existent. Therefore, one does not abandon them. Because they are not existent, one does not grasp them.

Thus, there is no obstruction regarding anything. Regarding the supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), those called "retributive powers" (*vipākābhijñā*) function with spontaneous mastery by relying on the power of non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpajñāna*).

Those called "cultivated powers" (*bhāvanābhijñā*) function with intentional mastery by relying on the power of the ultimate limit of meditative concentration (*prāntakoṭika-dhyāna*). Transformation...
Regarding "supernatural power" (abhijñā): because it relies on the fourteen transformations through the power of supernormal knowledge, it differs from the first two powers.

Regarding the mention of "knowledge of signlessness" (*animitta-jñāna*) within the tenth [power]: this is because one contemplates the principle of signlessness by means of analytical knowledge (*vikalpa-jñāna*); whereas the sixth perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*) is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpa*).
The following clarifies the virtues produced by this [perfection]. This section has three parts: the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion.

Regarding the heading, the mention of the "ten knowledges" (*daśajñāna*) refers to the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*) previously discussed; all ten are termed "knowledges" because they have been explained as such before.

This passage cites the fundamental source that gives rise to them, providing a general heading for the virtues produced. From the "seven riches" (*saptadhanas*) onwards, there is a detailed explanation of those produced virtues. Within this, there is...
Three [sections]. First, the explicit clarification of the virtues produced; second, the demonstration of the objects illuminated by them; third, the revelation of the obstacles removed by them.
Within the first [section], there are two parts: a specific explanation and a general summary. Within the specific explanation, eight gates are briefly presented.
The first clarifies the seven noble riches (*saptāryadhanāni*). All worthy sages employ these seven virtues to nurture the *dharmakāya* and provide sustenance for its benefit.
O Āyuṣmat, by employing these one attains Buddhahood; they are ultimately inexhaustible. For this reason, they are called the "Noble Wealth" (*āryadhana*).
Thus it is said that because the noble ones employ them to attain Buddhahood, they are called "wealth.

Although the virtues employed by the noble ones are manifold, the reason only seven are taken as the Noble Wealth is that faith is the foundation of all virtues, giving is the benefit that arises from faith, and ethical discipline is able to eliminate [transgressions].

Regarding the difficulty of acquiring wealth: one hears that it is possible to gather all manner of treasures; through shame (*hrī*), one honors and increases what is wholesome; through remorse (*apatrāpya*), one rejects and distances oneself from evil.
Wisdom (*prajñā*) can lead and guide the six kinds of wealth so that they increase, resulting in the abundance of the six noble and holy riches (*ṣaḍ-ārya-dhana*).
These seven are essential; therefore, these are called the "seven riches. Although this is the general explanation, as for the detailed classification therein: in this context...
It is produced by the seven riches and the ten perfections; therefore, only the preeminent forms of faith and so forth are taken up.
Within these seven, each contains ten aspects, as explained at length in the *Daśāvaivartika-dharmakṣānti-parivarta*. It asks: "What is the bodhisattva’s treasury of faith (*śraddhā-kośa*)?
This bodhisattva believes that all phenomena are empty and lack true reality; he believes that all phenomena are signless; he believes that all phenomena..."
It is wishless (*apraṇihita*). It is to believe that all phenomena are without an agent; to believe that all phenomena are unreal; to believe that all phenomena are without solidity;
to believe that all phenomena are immeasurable; to believe that all phenomena are unsurpassed; to believe that all phenomena are untranscendable;
to believe that all phenomena are unborn, and so forth, as explained at length. According to this, it clarifies profound faith in the profound Dharma.
1. Emptiness (*śūnyatā*): This refers to the absence of any real truth in that which is believed in; for the true merits of the Buddhas and Tathāgatas are non-existent. 2. Signlessness (*animitta*):

This refers to the fact that the physical marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*) of the Buddhas cannot be apprehended. 3. Wishlessness (*apraṇihita*): This refers to the emptiness of the sentient beings who are to be delivered by means of the great vows. 4. Non-agency (*anabhisaṃskāra*):
This refers to the fact that within the dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*), there is no agent capable of acting. 5. Unreality (*atattva*).

1. It is empty, because the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) space is not established as a substantial reality. 2. It is without solidity, because *nirvāṇa* is eternally abiding and lacks any solid substance. 3.
It is immeasurable, because the past is empty and there is no dharma to be further sought or measured through deliberation.
4. It is unsurpassed, because the future is empty and there is no superior dharma to be attained. 5. It is unfordable, because the present...
The ten directions are also empty, because they cannot be measured in terms of distance, such as near or far.

Regarding the "ten non-arising," the kalpas of the three periods of time are empty, because arising in the past, present, or future cannot be apprehended. One can thus believe that these ten kinds are all unapprehendable, yet without negating the existence of all phenomena.
As stated in the passage below: "All these are the inconceivable dharmas of the Buddhas."
The mind is not terrified; even to the point of entering all inconceivable eons, the mind remains unafraid.
Thus it is said that there are ten kinds of the wealth of faith, and the latter six are likewise.

Second, regarding the explanation of the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*): The *Bodhisattvabhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* asks, "What are the bodily, vocal, and mental actions of a bodhisattva that are subsumed under skillful means (*upāya*)?
They are the four means of attraction. Furthermore, for what reason are only the four means of attraction designated as "skillful means"?
It means that by means of these four kinds [of skillful means], bodhisattvas are universally able to embrace, discipline, and bring to maturity all sentient beings;
beyond these, there are none more excellent or more numerous. What are the names of these four kinds of skillful means?

First, the skillful means of conformity; second, the skillful means of embracing; third, the skillful means of causing entry; and fourth, the skillful means of conforming to their conduct. Why is this so? First—
One gives various kinds of material wealth as a gift to benefit sentient beings, desiring to cause them to listen to what is taught and to practice according to those instructions.

Next, one employs pleasant speech. Toward those who are deluded in various matters, one acts to eliminate all their delusions so that none remain, causing them to embrace and investigate correct principles. This is called being able to...

Regarding the inclusion of skillful means: if bodhisattvas, having understood the dispositions of those sentient beings and having scrutinized correct reasoning, subsequently engage in beneficial conduct (*artha-caryā*) to extract those beings from unwholesome states and to exhort, discipline, settle, and establish them in wholesome states—such beneficial conduct is called the skillful means of causing entry.
If bodhisattvas, through such skillful means, cause...
Once all sentient beings have entered [the path], he finally practices together with them in the same correct activities, causing them to follow along.
By these means, he ensures that those being transformed do not think:
"Since you yourself lack perfect pure faith, ethical discipline, and generosity, why rely on the good to exhort others, admonish, reproach, or censure them?"

One should maintain mindfulness. Therefore, it should be known that the Bodhisattva’s means of integration through commonality (*sādhārana-saṃgrahavastu*) is called the "expedient means of conformity.
Thus it is stated in the treatises. Now, although the sequence differs in this sutra’s mention of "benefiting, gentle speech, giving, and commonality," the actual practice should indeed be the same.
Third, the explanation of the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*): these are the four unimpeded knowledges, the meaning of which has been explained above.

Fourth, the explanation of the four reliances (*pratisaraṇa*): first, abandoning the worldly practices upon which sentient beings rely; second, abandoning worldly ornamental terminology and phrasing; third, abandoning the Buddha’s teachings of sutras of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*);
and fourth, abandoning the conceptual discrimination of the wisdom derived from hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*) regarding sutras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). As [it is said]:

Because one enters [the path] gradually and successively through these stages, as stated in the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*: "The basis refers to the four reliances, as explained at length in the sūtras.
First, rely on the Dharma and not on persons. This means that if a teaching is spoken by the Tathāgata or by his disciples—the twelvefold scripture—one should study and listen to it accordingly;
one does not practice according to the conduct of ordinary persons, nor does one follow them."
Second, relying on the meaning and not on the letter: this means that if a teaching cannot be expressed by other words, then the composed flowery phrases and syllables can only serve to clarify it;
they alone manifest the purity of the Dharma and the bright, white Brahma-faring. Within such a teaching, one should cultivate reverence, faith, and understanding.
It is not that which manifests a perverted holy life (*brahmacarya*), nor that which fails to clarify the holy life, but rather those flowery words and phrases composed merely for ornamentation.
Thirdly, one relies on sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and does not rely on sūtras of interpretable meaning (*neyārtha*;
specifically, regarding the Tathāgata’s teachings on the profound emptiness that accords with and conforms to dependent origination through conditions, one must not harbor false attachments).

It is said: "One should not abide in the mind of internal dogmatic attachment (*svāntar-dṛṣṭi-parāmarśa*) even toward the meaning of what is superficial. One should only be exhorted to investigate the sūtras of explicit meaning (*nītārtha*).

Relying on wisdom (*jñāna*), one does not rely on consciousness (*vijñāna*"; that is, one should not give rise to complacency through mere hearing and fail to progress in the practice of the Dharma in accordance with the Dharma.
Rather, for the sake of exhausting all outflows (*āsrava*), one is exhorted to seek the wisdom of personally realized inner truth)."

The fifth is the ten powers (*daśabala*); the sixth is the four fearlessnesses (*caturvaiśāradya*); the seventh is the six supernormal knowledges (*ṣaḍabhijñā*); and the eighth is the three types of clear knowledge (*tisro vidyāḥ*).
These four categories will be explained in the subsequent text; this is a detailed exposition. Next, regarding the phrase "merits of hundreds of thousands of millions of *asaṃkhyeya*s":
The second section provides a general summary.
The preceding first section correctly elucidated all the virtues that arise; from here begins the second section, which demonstrates the objects of focus.

This contains three parts: the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion. First, regarding the heading: it states that the wisdom arising in successive order can take the eight worldly truths as its object.
"All phenomena" refers to citing the illuminating wisdom to indicate the objects of its focus.

Since the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is signless and easily illuminated, we shall now only manifest the distinctions of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Second, there is a specific manifestation of the eight conventional dharmas:

first, the Four Truths (*catuḥsatya*), because each of the two categories—defiled and pure—possesses both fruit and cause; second, the Two Truths, wherein the two truths of the initial gate are both conventional truths.
Therefore: Third, the twelve links of dependent origination; their meaning is as previously explained. Fourth, conventional designation through causal conditioning (*pratyaya-saṃvṛti*);

for example, the aggregates (*skandha*) condition the formation of a conventionally designated person, and likewise the four sensory elements condition the formation of a conventionally designated pillar and so forth. As the sutras state: "Conventional phenomena formed by conditions are devoid of self, yet possess dharmas.

Fifth, conventional designation through mutual dependence (*apekṣā-saṃvṛti*). There are three types of mutual dependence: first, mutual dependence through aggregation (*saṃcita-apekṣā*), such as long and short.

1. Mutual dependence through mutual exclusion, such as blue and yellow. 2. Mutual dependence through mutual opposition, such as existence and non-existence; as the sutra says, "Because all characteristics are empty in their mutual dependence.
6. The provisional nature of continuity (*saṃtati-prajñapti*), which establishes a provisional entity based on preceding and succeeding moments of consciousness.
Because it is uninterrupted from beginning to end, as the sūtra says: "The continuity [of phenomena] is called 'one' because it is unobtainable.

Seventh is the conventional designation of dharmas (*dharma-prajñapti*). In a single moment, the mind and mental factors, as well as the various atoms of the four sense-objects and other such phenomena, arise from causes and emerge through the aggregation of conditions.
Apart from conditions there is no dharma; apart from dharmas there are no conditions. This is called "conventionality of causal arising" (*hetu-utpatti-prajñapti*), and it is also...

This is called the "provisional designation of dharmas" (*dharmaprajñapti*). As the Sūtra says: "Because of arising, there is origination. This means that while dharmas are not themselves conditions, they exist as a real collection of realities;

thus, they are called "produced dharmas. Regarding "existing as a real collection of realities": for example, a single atom is a reality within the provisional designation of being produced by conditions.

Furthermore, a moment (*kṣaṇa*) is a reality within the provisional designation of continuity. Because such realities aggregate together, it is said that they "exist as a real collection of realities. This refers to all [conditioned phenomena].

The ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*) is called a "dharma-designation" (*dharmaprajñapti*). Eighth is the "designation of sensation" (*vedanā-prajñapti*): just as when an ultimate atom is touched, it constitutes a coarse touch, thereby receiving the name "touch" and performing the function of contact (*sparśa*).
As it is said that the objects of touch (*spraṣṭavya-viṣaya*) are constituted by their own kind, the same should apply to the other [objects]—form, odor, and taste.

This differs from the previously mentioned "designation of dependent origination" (*pratyayopanibandha-prajñapti*), which is a designation based on the gathering of heterogeneous conditions, as described in the Sūtra on Dharmas.

It is called "provisional" (prajñapti) because it receives a name based on the arising of function; it is called a "composite phenomenon" (saṃskṛta-dharma) because various phenomena of the same kind gather together.
It is called a "constructed phenomenon" (kṛtaka-dharma) because the subtle constitutes the coarse. Within the three gates of the provisional, this is the third, termed the "provisional.
Since it has already been revealed as such, the existence of the two truths mentioned previously is not reiterated here; for the Middle Truth is precisely the meaning of the provisional. Therefore:
The following is the third summary: These eight categories all possess conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*); therefore, they are called the "eight conditioned dharmas.

However, among the Four Noble Truths, the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*)—which is the Truth of Non-existence (*abhāva-satya*) within the Two Truths—is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) within the context of dependent designation.

Although these three are not conditioned, they are generally termed "conditioned" by way of majority rule. As for "original wisdom" (*mūla-jñāna*), it refers to the time of entering meditative observation, when [the two truths] are simultaneously...
Regarding the wisdom that illuminates [the internal], it is called "fundamental wisdom" (mūla-jñāna) in contrast to the wisdom that emerges from contemplation (vyutthāna-jñāna).

Because these eight—all of which are termed conventional dharmas (saṃvṛti-dharma)—are illuminated both internally by the wisdom of internal measurement and externally by the wisdom of peripheral illumination, the wisdom that emerges from contemplation likewise illuminates these eight.
However, fundamental wisdom is specifically mentioned because it clearly manifests the capacity to counteract obstacles; for the wisdom that emerges from contemplation does not sever those obstacles.

The following section is the third, which clarifies the obstacles to be eliminated. This contains three parts: the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion. First, regarding the statement "furthermore, that which can be eliminated by this wisdom":

this refers to the fact that the aforementioned fundamental wisdom eliminates obstacles. From the "five hindrances" (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*) downward, the various obstacles—both causes and effects—and their attendant afflictions are specifically revealed as the objects to be eliminated.
Herein, eighteen types of phenomena are briefly enumerated. Regarding the "eight inversions" (*aṣṭa-viparyāsa*):

This is because there are four inversions regarding the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and four inversions regarding the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*). As for the nine afflictions (*nava āghātāḥ*), they refer to the nine bases of affliction.
These nine bases consist of three sets of three, making nine: (1) those who harm my loved ones; (2) those who hate my dear friends; and (3) those who are currently afflicting me.

Since these apply to the three periods of time, they constitute nine afflictions. The other categories are as commonly explained. Regarding the "four fetters" (*catvāraḥ saṃyojanāni*), they are as follows:

These are the four fetters (*saṃyojana*), as explained in the Abhidharma (*Abhidharma*). Regarding the statement in the section on the "afflictions of vexation" (*upāyāsa-saṃyojana*) that they are all called "unwholesome" (*akuśala*): it is because they all contradict the true goodness of *nirvāṇa*.

The three preceding sections together constitute the second part, which specifically clarifies what is produced. From the "ten knowledges" (*daśajñāna*) downward is the third section, which provides a concluding exhortation.

As for the phrase "that which is to be eliminated by the objects of the ten knowledges," this refers to the objects of the ten knowledges, namely, the eight dharmas of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

Excluded by the ten knowledges (*daśajñāna*) are the eighteen unwholesome factors; these are cited as non-causes. All other remaining meritorious qualities are called causes of Buddhahood, and therefore they should be practiced.
As for the eight worldly dharmas (*aṣṭau lokadharmāḥ*), they are not called causes because their objective sphere (*viṣayadvāra*) does not possess the meaning of being a cause.
