First, the second section below clarifies the fruit (*phala*). This passage consists of three parts: the restatement of the question, the explanation, and the conclusion. Within the second part, the explanation, there are also three sections:

first, the clarification of the fruit of essence (*svabhāva-phala*); second, the explanation of the fruit of meaning (*artha-phala*); and third, a further elucidation of both the fruits of essence and meaning.
The beginning and middle [of this section] have two parts: first, clarifying the characteristic of the single essence; second, revealing the gateway of the two bodies.

Within the first of these, there are also two: first, citing the cause to indicate the fruit; second, correctly clarifying the essence of the fruit. Regarding the statement in the first part that "it is the essential nature," this is because it is the single Dharma-realm.
As for the term "its essence" below, it correctly reveals the non-dual characteristic. Within this, there are also two: the specific revelation.
General Explanation. First, there are two sets of seven pairs specifically revealed. Regarding "neither existent nor non-existent":

it is not that there is a single substantial entity of the fruit, yet it is not that there is no single substantial entity of the fruit. Regarding "neither large nor small": it enters into a single atom without leaving anything out, yet it encompasses the worlds of the ten directions while remaining beyond them.
Regarding "neither body nor mind": it is free from physical forms such as long and short, and free from states such as existence and non-existence.

Because it is the object of contemplation, it is neither a characteristic nor belongs to the three periods of time; this is because it is free from the characteristics of "this" or "that" place, and free from the passing away of prior or subsequent time.
It is neither a celestial being nor a human being; this is because it does not abide in the heights of space, nor does it abide in the lower realms.

It is neither a name nor is it permanence, bliss, self, or purity; this is because it cannot be praised by fragrant names, nor can it be taken as a refuge through sublime virtues. It is not among the six realms...
Regarding the "entry into the six consciousnesses": it is not produced by good or evil, nor can it be grasped as name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*).

Because it transcends all numerical and quantitative phenomena and all marks of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), this summarizes the preceding seven pairs. It is neither a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) nor a ghost or spirit (*bhūta*).
Because there is neither merit nor transgression; "neither moving nor still" means there is neither distraction nor concentration;

"neither arising nor ceasing, neither the primary nor the secondary" means it is neither conventional nor ultimate; "neither the five colors, nor the six elements, nor the field" means it is neither particular nor universal;
"neither the dharma-realm nor the three realms" means it is neither the root nor the branch; "neither bound nor liberated" means it is undefiled.
Because it is impure; because it is neither luminous nor dark, being neither wise nor foolish; because it is not an attainment of a dharma that is quiescent and unconditioned.
This summarizes the preceding seven pairs. It is called "quiescent" because it is far removed from the characteristics of the two extremes of these seven pairs.
It is called "unconditioned" because, although it is free from the two extremes, it does not constitute a "middle. For this reason, it is not an attained dharma. (1)
The following section is the second general explanation, which contains two parts: the formal exposition and the dispelling of doubts.

Regarding the first part, the phrase "beyond all phenomena" refers to transcending the aforementioned two sets of seven pairs of all phenomena. As for the phrase "the cessation of the sphere of mental activity":
The renunciation of all phenomena is itself free from that renunciation, for there is nothing upon which it can rely.
That its state is difficult to measure is because, although it is not an attainment, it is not a non-attainment either. Next, regarding the dispelling of doubts:

there are those who harbor suspicions, saying, "If this is indeed so—that the mind and words are cut off—why did the Tathāgata grant the prediction to the Bodhisattva, saying that he shall practice various deeds for such-and-such eons, and at such-and-such..."
"One will attain Buddhahood in the world. Is this not showing the future fruit?

To dispel such doubts, it is said that by practicing for the duration of an eon within the realm of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), there is a karmic fruition. This "fruition" refers to the fruition of the pure land, the physical body, and the marks and signs of excellence.
All of these are explained from the perspective of conventional truth. Now, what is being discussed here is outside of the two truths. Because...

Below this, the second section clarifies the gateway of the two bodies (*dvikāya*). This section contains two parts: first, the formal elucidation of the Tathāgata’s two bodies.
The second [section] clarifies the two bodies of the lower stages. The first [of these] contains four propositions: first, the general; second, the specific clarification;

This clarifies that the *dharmakāya* (fruit-body) is eternally abiding because it is free from arising and ceasing; the *nirmāṇakāya* (response-body) is likewise eternal and free from arising and ceasing, differing from the two bodies of bodhisattvas which are impermanent.

Summary. The first part also has two sections: first, clarifying that the two bodies of the Bodhisattva are impermanent; second, revealing that the two bodies of ordinary beings are different.

From "O Son of the Buddha" onwards, the fruit of the meaning (*artha-phala*) is explained next. This section has three parts: a general heading, a detailed explanation, and a third part which is the summary.

Regarding the first part, as for what is called the "merit of the meaning": its essential nature is a fruit that is wondrously transcendent, free from characteristics, unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and effortless (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
Because it is simply without anything to be done, there is nothing it does not do; it acts for the benefit of all sentient beings. Thus, it emerges from within the single essence.
Immeasurable meanings and immeasurable merits; because these qualities and meanings are accumulated, they are called a "body" (*kāya*).

This is precisely the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body). As stated in the passage below regarding the *dharmakāya*: dwelling within this stage of wondrous enlightenment, there are only manifestations that can be named.
There are immeasurable meanings and immeasurable names, yet their emergence is of one essence—namely, the eternally abiding purity of the wondrous fruit. As for...
Space is inconceivable, ineffable, incalculable, and cannot be designated as an entrance, because its constituent elements (dhātu) can be discerned.
Regarding the statement that "the path of all Buddhas is identical and their resultant dharmas are not different," this is because the ten titles and other virtues are common to all Buddhas.
This is what is specifically clarified in the second section below, wherein eighty-eight virtues are briefly manifested.

First, the ten titles [of the Buddha] are clarified. However, regarding these ten titles, the sūtras and śāstras differ: in some places the Buddha is said to be the tenth, while in others he is said to be the ninth.

In this present sūtra, the explanation follows the former method. First, as for "Tathāgata": [Note: The provided source text ends with "一如來者" (First, as for "Tathāgata"), indicating that the full definition of each title would follow in the subsequent portion of the original text.]
The *Daśanāma-sūtra* states: "I am that which is called 'Thus' (tathā), and that which is called 'Thus' is I. The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* states:
"All Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, come from the six pāramitās, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, and the eleven emptinesses to reach Great Nirvāṇa;
the Tathāgata is likewise. For this reason, the Buddha is titled the Tathāgata. The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says: "Because his words are without falsehood."

He is named Tathāgata. The *Buddhatva-śāstra* states: "From the stage of abiding in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāvavihāra*) up to the attainment of realization (*prāpti-lābha*), he is therefore called Tathāgata.
Second, regarding the Arhat (*arhat*): the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Having already attained all that ought to be attained, he is worthy of being the unsurpassed field of merit for the world;
he is worthy of receiving the respect and offerings of all beings. For these reasons, he is called 'Arhat'. Third, the Samyaksaṃbuddha (Perfectly Complete Knower).

Regarding this, the treatise states: "In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), he awakens to all offerings; therefore, he is called the Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksaṃbuddha*). Fourth, regarding the one endowed with the perfection of knowledge and conduct (*vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna*):

the treatise states that "knowledge" refers to the three knowledges (*tisro vidyāḥ*). "Conduct" is as explained in the sūtras: because the two categories of tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are perfectly fulfilled, he is said to be "endowed with the perfection of knowledge and conduct.
Fifth, regarding the Sugata: the treatise states that he has ascended to the ultimate limit and never again returns.

Therefore, he is named Sugata (Well-Gone). Sixth, regarding "Knower of the World" (*lokavid*): the treatise states that because he thoroughly knows all aspects of the defiled and pure characteristics of both the world and the realm of sentient beings, he is called the Knower of the World.
Seventh, regarding "Unsurpassed Being" (*anuttara*): the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says, "An 'upper being' is defined by that which is to be severed;
one who has nothing further to sever is called an Unsurpassed Being. Of all the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, there is none...

Because there are no afflictions (*kleśa*), there is nothing to be abandoned. For this reason, the Buddha is titled the Unsurpassed Person (*anuttara-puruṣa*). Furthermore, "superior person" (*puruṣa*) refers to one who engages in dispute;
an "unsurpassed person" has no dispute. The Tathāgata is without dispute; for this reason, the Buddha is titled the Unsurpassed Person.

This is explained at length in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "One is already a great man (*mahāpuruṣa*). [The text continues: "The eight types of taming men... and so forth. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Being oneself already a great man..."
Furthermore, regarding the "taming of the man": O son of good family, that which is called a Tathāgata is truly neither a man nor not a man;
it is because he tames men that the Tathāgata is called a man. Son of good family, all men and women who possess four qualities are called "men.
What are these four? First, a virtuous friend (kalyāṇamitra); second, the ability to listen to the Dharma; third, reflection...
It is only through righteousness. Fourth, practicing as taught. If a man or a woman is endowed with these four dharmas, they are called a "great man" (*puruṣa*).
If there is a man who lacks these four dharmas, he cannot be called a great man. Why is this? Although his body is that of a man, his conduct is like that of a beast.
The Tathāgata disciplines both men and women; therefore, the Buddha is titled the "Tamer" (*vināyaka*).
“Great Man” (*puruṣa*), and so forth, as explained at length. In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, these two titles are combined into a single phrase:
“The sole Great Man in all the world who thoroughly knows the supreme skillful means for taming the mind; therefore, he is called the Unsurpassed Great Man, the Tamer of Men.
Regarding the title “Teacher of Gods and Humans,” the treatise states: “Because he is the true eye, because he is true wisdom, because he is true...”
Because it is the meaning; because it is the ultimate reality; because it serves as the introduction to the explicit meaning;
because it serves as the basis for all meanings; because it renders the implicit meaning explicit; because it is able to sever the doubts that arise;
because it is able to reveal the profound depths; because it brings about clarity and purity; because it is the root of all phenomena; and because it opens [the way].
Because he is a guide and because he serves as the basis [for others], he is able to correctly instruct and teach devas and humans, enabling them to transcend all suffering;

therefore, the Buddha is called the Teacher of Devas and Humans (*śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām*). According to the commentary: he is the "True Eye" because he possesses the wisdom of the path of realization (*darśanamārga*) that perceives things directly;
he is the "True Knower" because he possesses the wisdom of the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) capable of definitive discernment; and he is the "True Meaning."
Because he reveals the ineffable meaning of all phenomena; because for those who seek the true Dharma, he establishes the unerring teaching through words.
The following six phrases may be understood by reversing this. One who possesses these ten qualities is called a teacher. As for the ten Buddhas:

The Treatise says: "Regarding the collection of dharmas that lead to what is beneficial, the collection of dharmas that lead to what is not beneficial, and the collection of dharmas that lead to neither the beneficial nor the non-beneficial—one attains manifest and complete awakening toward them in every respect."
Therefore, he is named "Buddha. According to the commentary, this reveals his possession of all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvajñā*).

Because each of these three aggregates (*trikaṇḍaka*) permeates the categories of wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate, and because the Buddha alone fully awakens to them in their entirety, it is so called. The concluding summary below states:
"Because he possesses the ten virtues mentioned above, he is one who is honored by all sentient beings. This is the general meaning of the term "World-Honored One" (*Bhagavān*). If, by means of...
This is called the tenth [name]. As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi*, he is named Bhagavān because he possesses all-encompassing merit and is able to shatter the great armies of all Māras.
Next, to clarify the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*): these three sets of six qualities are not shared with ordinary arhats;

therefore, they are called "unique. Regarding the first six, the quality of being without faults that is not shared [with others] means that for an arhat, all outflows (*āsrava*) have been eternally exhausted.
When entering a village to wander for alms, he may at times travel along a road together with wicked elephants or vicious dogs;
or, while in the forest retreat (*āraṇyaka*), he might abandon the correct path and walk upon a wrong or evil track.
Such errors of an Arhat do not exist at all in the Tathāgata. Therefore, it is said that his body is without fault. Furthermore:
An Arhat may, at times, due to forgetfulness (*muṣitasmṛti*), suffer a lapse in his duties;
such forgetfulness is forever absent in a Tathāgata. Therefore, it is said that his mindfulness is without loss.
Furthermore, an Arhat may, at any time, lose his way while in a forest hermitage (*āraṇyaka*), or enter an empty place and cry out loudly with clamorous noise.
He may hear sounds, or perhaps due to habitual tendencies, he may smile with upturned lips and bared teeth with a joyful air, his mind untainted by defilement.
Regarding all such types of harsh sounds, the Tathāgata is forever free from them; therefore, it is said that his speech is without fault.
One who is free from divergent thoughts is like an arhat, who within the realm of saṃsāra with remainder gives rise exclusively to a mind of revulsion,
and within the realm of nirvāṇa without remainder gives rise exclusively to the thought of tranquility.
The Tathāgata has no perception of differentiation therein, because he abides in the supreme equanimity of relinquishment (*upekṣā*). He has no unconcentrated mind;

unlike an Arhat, who is said to be "in concentration" when entering meditative equipoise (*samāpatti*) and "not in concentration" when emerging from it, the Tathāgata possesses no unconcentrated mind throughout all states.
Consequently, he has no state of equanimity based on non-cognition.
This is because, like an Arhat who fails to exercise skillful discernment and consequently abandons the work of benefiting sentient beings,
the Tathāgata never possesses such a deficiency.

Regarding the next six points on "no diminution": just as an Arhat, by virtue of the purification of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), may undergo a decline from what has not yet been attained—such as a decline in mindfulness, aspiration, and even knowledge and vision—analogous retrogression is forever absent in the Tathāgata; therefore, it is said that his mindfulness is without diminution, and so forth.

Among these, the first four are the paths that serve as the antidotes to the obscurations regarding the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*). The latter two do not diminish the fruits attained thereby;
because the Tathāgata’s causes are perfected and his fruits are complete, there is no diminution in these respects.
Regarding the latter six dharmas: just as an Arhat at times engages in wholesome bodily action or engages in neutral action, so too should one understand his vocal and mental actions.
This is because the Tathāgata’s three types of action are preceded by wisdom and follow after wisdom.
There is no indeterminate [state]. Furthermore, regarding all objects of knowledge throughout the three periods of time, an Arhat cannot understand them through a mere casual mental engagement;
therefore, their knowledge and vision are said to be "possessing attachment," as they cannot achieve a complete and exhaustive correct understanding of everything.

Therefore, it is called "possessing resistance. When the Tathāgata directs his attention even briefly toward the objects of the three periods of time, he is able to correctly comprehend the distinctions among all knowable things and phenomena.
As for the statement in this sutra that "the bodily action follows wisdom," and so forth:
This is because of the wisdom that precedes [the practice] and the wisdom that accompanies it. Regarding the knowledge that within the three times there are "obstructions" (*sāvaraṇa*):

this is because, apart from those [obstructions], one cannot be free from the obstruction to complete and correct understanding. Regarding "unobstructed" (*anāvaraṇa*): this is because, apart from those [obstructions], one cannot be subject to the attachment of immediate and spontaneous understanding.
These points are explained in detail as they appear in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*. That text states: "In this context, the first four are 'non-forgetfulness' (*asaṃpramoṣa*)."
The loss of the Dharma and that which is comprised of the extraction of habitual tendencies are included [in the first category]. Next, one is comprised of great compassion.
The remainder should be known as being comprised of the sublime wisdom of all modes.
Next, the ten powers (*daśabala*) are explained. Based on these ten knowledges (*jñāna*), there are ten matters that can subdue false doctrines; therefore, they are called "powers.

Regarding the power of what is possible and what is impossible (*sthānāsthāna-bala*): it is the thorough penetration, in accordance with reality, of all causes and effects as to what is possible and what is impossible.
If any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas propound the non-existence of cause and effect, or the doctrine of unequal causes and effects, [this power] is able to suppress them and bring them under control.

This constitutes a point of defeat (*nigrahasthāna*). This matter is established by virtue of that first power. Regarding the power of karma (*karmabala*): the Tathāgata knows and perceives that one experiences the fruits of one's own karma;
there is no such thing as performing an action oneself while another receives its fruit.

If śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas propound false doctrines and teachings, claiming that karma can be transcended or that the experience [of its results] can be transcended, he is able to subdue them and cause them to fall into a point of defeat. This matter is established by virtue of the power of knowledge regarding karma (*karmajñānabala*).
It is accomplished. Regarding the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*): the Tathāgata’s teaching manifests three wheels: first, the wheel of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-cakra*);

second, the wheel of reading minds (*ādeśanā-cakra*); and third, the wheel of instruction and admonition (*anuśāsana-cakra*). By training and guiding his disciples, he brings about the assembly of the noble ones (*ārya-saṃgha*).

If there are śramaṇas or brahmins who harbor a competitive spirit, propound contrary doctrines, or oppose the authentic scriptures, he is able to subdue them and cause them to fall into defeat. This...

This matter is accomplished through the power of knowledge regarding the determination of causal conditions (*nidāna-jñānabala*). As for the power of the faculties (*indriya-bala*): the Tathāgata thoroughly understands superior, middling, and inferior faculties;

he teaches the Dharma accordingly so that they may plant the seeds, bring them to maturity, and attain liberation. This matter is accomplished through the power of knowledge regarding the faculties (*indriya-jñānabala*).
Regarding the power of aspiration (*chanda-bala*): the Tathāgata perceives the three classes of sentient beings;

having seen their inclinations toward the false or the correct as they truly are, he eradicates evil aspirations and increases wholesome aspirations. This matter is accomplished through the power of the knowledge of aspiration. Regarding the power of nature (*gotra-bala*):

the Tathāgata observes and knows the spiritual lineages (*gotra*) of sentient beings—whether coarse, middling, or sublime—and causes these three types of persons to enter their respective lineages in accordance with the principle.

The various dharma-gates are accomplished through the power of knowledge regarding the causes of phenomena (*hetu-jñāna-bala*). As for the power of the fruit (*phala-bala*), it is called elsewhere the "power of the path leading to the destination" (*yathāsthāna-gāminī-pratipad-bala*).
The Tathāgata clearly perceives that the dharmas of the path to transcendence result in the fruit of liberation, while the dharmas of obstructing paths result in the fruit of saṃsāra;

he causes [beings] to extinguish those obstacles to the path and cultivate the path to transcendence. This is the matter accomplished by the power of the fruit. [Next is] the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*).
Regarding power: it is also called the power of knowledge regarding birth and death in other contexts.

The Tathāgata clearly perceives all sentient beings dying here and being born there, and grants them predictions in accordance with reality. If any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas hold to the view of annihilationism, he is able to subdue them and cause them to fall into defeat.
This is what is accomplished by the power of the divine eye. Regarding the power of recollecting past lives: the Tathāgata clearly understands...
He perceives past lives and recounts events of the past in order to inspire a sense of revulsion and fear in sentient beings.

If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who cling to the view of eternalism, he is able to subdue them and cause them to fall into defeat. This is what is accomplished through the power of knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsajñānabala*).

As for the power of the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣayabala*), the Tathāgata himself knows that his liberation is unimpeded and thoroughly realized; even those with overweening pride [cannot challenge him].
If śramaṇas or brahmins who have not yet attained arhatship claim to have already attained it, [the Tathāgata] is able to subdue them and cause them to fall into defeat;
this is an accomplishment resulting from the power of the exhaustion of outflows (āsravakṣaya-bala). This is explained in detail as set forth in the *Anuttarāśraya-sūtra*.
Next, the four immeasurables are explained: namely, loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*).
Their meanings are as explained above. Next are the four fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*): "I am an omniscient one" is the fearlessness of being omniscient;

"my outflows are exhausted" is the fearlessness of having exhausted the outflows; and "the path of untainted deliverance from afflictions" is the fearlessness of proclaiming the path leading to the exhaustion of suffering.
Fearlessness. Regarding "fearlessness in teaching the obstacles to the path": this refers to the fearlessness in explaining those things that obstruct the path.

Among these, the first two [types of fearlessness] consist of the teacher’s own perfection of wisdom and abandonment, while the latter two cause others to achieve the perfection of wisdom and abandonment. This is what is meant by the statement in the treatise: "The teacher and the disciples are both perfected in wisdom and abandonment.
This is precisely what is being described here.

Next, the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) are explained, as previously described. Next, the five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*) are explained. The meaning of the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcāṅga-dharmakāya*) is as commonly explained.

Next, the three types of faultless karma (*anavadya-karman*) are explained; these refer to the three kinds of purity of the Tathāgata, and are thus called "faultless. As the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
"When the Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, attained Bodhi, he dwelt in the Buddha’s skillful means and attained all [qualities] for the sake of all sentient beings."
They attain a body equal to birth and so forth; they attain a body equal to all phenomena (*dharma*); they attain a body equal to all lands (*kṣetra*);
they attain a body equal to all three periods of time; they attain a body equal to all Tathāgatas; they attain a body equal to all Buddhas; they attain a body equal to all languages;
they attain a body equal to the entire realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*); they attain a body equal to the realm of empty space; they attain the unimpeded realm of phenomena.

Equal to the body [of the Tathāgata], they attain bodies equal to immeasurable [beings]; they attain bodies equal to the realm of all practices; they attain bodies equal to the realm of tranquil nirvāṇa.
O Son of the Buddha, you should know that the voice and the unimpeded mind follow the body attained by the Tathāgata.
It is likewise so. The Tathāgata is fully endowed with these three kinds of pure infinities.
According to the commentary: herein, the thirteenfold body is the faultless bodily karma; the thirteenfold voice is the faultless vocal karma;
and the thirteenfold mind is the faultless mental karma. Because they are faultless, they are without obstruction; being without obstruction...
Because it is unimpeded, it is without limit.

This also clarifies the Three Jewels (*triratna*). For whatever they manifest, there is nothing that does not accord with the profound principle; they pervade the six realms of existence and are ever in harmony with them.
As previously stated, the meaning of the Three Jewels for Bodhisattvas is the same, yet those [Bodhisattva Jewels] are not yet perfected and are not eternal. Now...
This refers to the perfectly consummate and eternally abiding Triple Gem. As the Vaipulya sutras state: "Within the single Gem of the Buddha, there are already the Dharma and the Sangha.
This is what is meant.

Next, regarding the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*): it is the cessation revealed through the severance of the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āvasthā*), as found within the fourfold gate of the Truths.
This is precisely the Great Purity Perfection (*mahā-viśuddhi-pāramitā*).
Next, regarding liberation (*vimokṣa*), it refers to unimpeded liberation (*anāvaraṇa-vimokṣa*). There are ten kinds of this, as stated in the Great Sūtra:
"All Buddhas possess ten kinds of unimpeded liberations. What are these ten? First, within a single atom, they are able to universally..."
First, they manifest the appearance in the world of unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddhas.
Second, within a single atom, they are able to universally manifest unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddhas turning the pure wheel of Dharma.
Third, within a single atom, they teach, transform, and subdue unspeakably unspeakable numbers of sentient beings. Fourth, within a single atom, they universally manifest...
5. To bestow prophecies upon unspeakably unspeakable numbers of transformation bodhisattvas within a single atom;
6. To universally manifest the appearance of all Buddhas of the three periods of time within a single atom;
7. To universally manifest all Buddha-lands of the three periods of time within a single atom; 8. To universally manifest... within a single atom.

The sovereign spiritual powers of all Buddhas of the three periods of time are as follows: ninth, within a single minute particle, they universally manifest all sentient beings of the three periods of time;
tenth, within a single minute particle, they universally manifest the Buddha-activities of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
These are the ten kinds of unimpeded liberation of all Buddhas.

Next, regarding "numinous wisdom" (*lingzhi*): that which is profoundly mysterious and difficult to fathom is the meaning of numinous wisdom; that which gives rise to [all things] without end is the meaning of numinous wisdom.
This has ten aspects, as stated in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*: "All Buddhas possess ten kinds of wisdom for giving rise to, abiding in, and maintaining [the Dharma]. What are these ten?
First, although all teachings are without any point of departure, they are able to give rise to purity."
1. The wisdom of aspiration (*praṇidhijñāna*). 2. All phenomena are without body, yet they are able to give rise to the wisdom of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
3. All Buddhas are entirely non-dual, yet they give rise to perfect awakening and realize all phenomena. 4.
All phenomena are entirely without self and without sentient beings, yet they are able to give rise to the wisdom that transforms sentient beings. 5. All phenomena are entirely...
1. While there are no marks, one is able to give rise to the wisdom of various marks. 2.
While all worlds are entirely without formation or destruction, one is able to give rise to the wisdom of the formation and destruction of worlds. 3.
While all dharmas have no creator, one is able to give rise to the wisdom of karmic retribution. 4. While all dharmas are inexpressible, one is able to give rise to the teaching of the Dharma.
1. The knowledge of the realms (*dhātu-jñāna*). 2. All phenomena are without defilement or purity, yet they can give rise to the wisdom of defilement and purity.
3. All phenomena are without arising or ceasing, yet they can give rise to the wisdom of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
These are the ten kinds of wisdom that give rise [to further insights].

Next, regarding the "One Vehicle" (Ekayāna): it refers to those who have planted roots of goodness under the Buddha; they all have no other destination, as none fail to reach the fruit of Great Parinirvāṇa together.
Therefore, the virtues of the Buddha are called the One Vehicle. To clarify this meaning, three metaphors are presented.
As stated in the Mahāvaipulya Sūtra: "For example, it is like a man who eats a small amount of diamond;
it is never digested, but must pass through his body until it reaches the vajra-wheel, whereupon it comes to rest. Why is this? Because that diamond is indestructible."

In this way, O Son of the Buddha, by planting even a small root of goodness toward the Tathāgata, one is able to destroy all conditioned afflictions, until finally reaching the ultimate wisdom of the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa, after which one abides. Why is this?
Because the roots of goodness planted toward the Tathāgata are inexhaustible. O Son of the Buddha, it is like Mount Sumeru and the great dry land...
A heap of grass: if someone were to hold a fire the size of a mustard seed, it would be able to burn it all away.
Why? Because the nature of fire is such that it can burn everything. It is just so with even a small root of goodness planted toward the Tathāgata;
it is able to burn away and extinguish all afflictions without remainder, leading to ultimate nirvāṇa. Why? Because [the merit] planted toward the Tathāgata...

Because the nature of their roots of goodness is ultimate, O Son of the Buddha, it is like this: for example, on the Snowy Mountains there is a great king of medicines named "Excellent Appearance" (Sudṛśa).
If anyone sees it, their eyes attain purity; if anyone hears it, their ears attain purity;
if anyone smells its fragrance, their nose attains purity; if anyone tastes its flavor, their tongue attains purity; and if anyone touches it, their body attains purity.
If one takes the soil from that ground, it can entirely eliminate immeasurable illnesses, bringing peace, security, and happiness.
The Tathāgata, the Perfectly Awakened One, the Unsurpassed King of Medicine, is likewise: he constantly benefits sentient beings through all manner of skillful means.
If there are those who behold the physical body of the Tathāgata, their eyes attain purity; if there are those who hear the name of the Tathāgata...
[Their] ears attain purity. If there are those who smell the fragrance of the Tathāgata’s precepts, their noses attain purity.

If there are those who taste the flavor of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, their tongues attain purity; they obtain the adamantine, broad, and long faculty of the tongue, capable of articulating all sounds and voices.
If there are those who touch the light of the Tathāgata, those persons immediately attain purity.

The physical body [is transcended], and one ultimately attains the unsurpassed Dharma-body. If there are those who mindfully recollect the Tathāgata, they shall attain the Buddha-remembrance Samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*) and their right mindfulness shall remain undisturbed.

If there are those who obtain a copy of this sūtra, or who prostrate to and make offerings at the ground where the Tathāgata’s stūpa-temple stands, those sentient beings will be fully endowed with roots of goodness, extinguish the afflictions and calamities, and attain the fruits of the noble ones (*ārya*). O Son of the Buddha, even...
Sentient beings who hold false views, upon seeing or hearing the Buddha, plant roots of goodness within that very act of seeing and hearing;
the karmic fruit of this is not in vain, leading ultimately to *nirvāṇa*, where all evils are severed and roots of goodness are fully perfected. This is explained at length:
this is called the merit of the Tathāgata’s Single Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
Next, regarding the Vajra-Treasury: the Buddha possesses ten kinds of firm and solid *dharmaratna* (Dharma-jewels). Their accumulation is called a "treasury. As stated in the Great Sūtra:
"All Buddhas possess ten kinds of qualities of a firm and solid hero (*vīradharma*). What are these ten? First, all vows are firm and cannot be thwarted or destroyed;
as it is said, their practice accords with their words. Second, they cultivate [these qualities] throughout all kalpas until the end of the future."
The Bodhisattva’s practice of the adornment of merit is never subject to fear.
Third, for the sake of transforming all sentient beings, they travel to unspeakably unspeakable numbers of worlds, teaching and transforming beings without any hindrance.

Fourth, toward sentient beings who either have faith or lack faith, they regard them with equal great compassion, without distinction. Fifth, from the first generation of the mind of enlightenment until the stage of right...
1. Awakening: During this interval, he never regressed or lost the bodhicitta. 2.
Cultivating all merits, he dedicated them entirely toward omniscience (*sarvākārajñatā*), seeking no worldly activities. 3.

He followed and trained in the physical, verbal, and mental actions of all Buddhas, forever abandoning the mind of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. 4. He impartially and universally illumined immeasurable and boundless [realms].
1. The Buddha’s True Dharma; 2. Purifying and attaining the bodhisattva mind; 3. Ultimately fulfilling all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*);
4. Being able to completely relinquish all worldly things; 5. Causing all sentient beings to extinguish all sufferings and attain the peaceful joy of equanimity;
6. Undergoing immeasurable suffering for the sake of all sentient beings; 7. Desiring to establish the lineage of all Buddhas; 8. Transcending [the world].
Birth and death; attaining the stage of the ten powers—these are the ten kinds of dharmas of the steadfast heroes of all Buddhas.
This is what is called the "Vajra Treasure Store."

Next, regarding the *dharmakāya-garbha*: it is called the *dharmakāya-garbha* because it is the accumulation of the manifold virtues of the *dharmakāya* of the response and transformation bodies (*nirmāṇa-dharmakāya*).
One interpretation states that the *dharmakāya-garbha* is so named because it is the accumulation of the five characteristics and five virtues. As the *Anuttarāśrayasūtra* says:
"The first body is endowed with five kinds of characteristics and five kinds of virtues. What are the five kinds of characteristics? First, [it is] non-..."
[They are] first, being inseparable; second, being non-separate; third, being free from the two extremes; fourth, being liberated from all hindrances;
and fifth, being pure by nature. What are the five kinds of qualities? First, immeasurability; second, incalculability;
third, inconceivability; fourth, uniqueness; and fifth, ultimate purity. Thus, these ten dharmas are in correspondence.
Because it is free [from defilements], it is called the "Dharmakāya-treasury.
Next, regarding the "wondrous treasury of intrinsic purity," this refers to the boundless merits of all Tathāgatas, which are unimpeded in every respect.

It penetrates both the defiled and the pure. When it resides in the stage of delusion (*kleśa-bhūmi*) yet remains undefiled, it is called "pure" (*viśuddha*); when it resides in the stage of purity yet is not [merely] pure, it is called "sublime" (*praṇīta*).
Therefore, it is named the "Treasury of Innate Purity and Sublimity. As stated in the *Anuttarāśrayasūtra*: "In what way is the Tathāgata inconceivable in his merits?
The boundless merits of all Tathāgatas throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges reside within delusion..."
The ground and the pure ground are mutually inclusive and correspond with one another; they have never been separate. They are neither defiled nor pure, for they are inconceivable.
Next, regarding the three types of penetration (*vidyā*): it means penetrating the beginningless past without exception, and penetrating the boundless future without limit.
Furthermore, because one ultimately penetrates the infinite dharma-realms of the ten directions in the present, it is called the Threefold Clarity (*trividya*).
Moreover, because one penetrates that every single thought-moment (*kṣaṇa*) of phenomena is not without the three kinds of the three periods of time, it is called the Threefold Clarity.
This is as explained in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* regarding the nine periods of time.

Regarding the next three unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), the *Ratnaketuparivarta Sūtra* (Renwang jing) states: "That which is non-dual within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is the unconditioned of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-asaṃskṛta*).

Because all marks (*nimitta*) are extinguished by taking principle as the object, it is the signless unconditioned of the extinction through the object of wisdom (*jñānālambana-nirodha-animitta-asaṃskṛta*).

When abiding in the stage of initial patience (*kṣānti*), immeasurable future births and deaths are not extinguished by means of the object of wisdom; therefore, it is the non-extinction through the object of wisdom (*ajñānālambana-nirodha*)."

Regarding the "unconditioned nature of characteristics" (*lakṣaṇāsaṃskṛta*): according to the examination of that sūtra, it refers to the first bhūmi and thus describes only a partial portion of the three unconditioned virtues.
In this present sūtra, however, it describes the virtues of a Buddha; therefore, it refers to the complete perfection of the three unconditioned virtues.
Next, regarding the three types of illumination (*vidyā*): as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, the illumination of the bodhisattvas refers to the various *prajñāpāramitās*;
the illumination of the Buddhas refers to the Buddha-eye; and the illumination of non-illumination (*avidyā-vidyā*) refers to ultimate emptiness (*atyanta-śūnyatā*).

According to this, if one discusses their distinct stages: the first illumination pertains to the stage of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi*); the second pertains to the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*); and the third illumination pertains to both cause and fruit. Regarding these...

These gates of penetration all reside within the stage of Buddhahood. Why is this? The gate of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna) that illumines the Buddha-nature of the single Dharma-realm is called the Buddha-eye;
it is the illumination of all Buddhas. The gate of the Wondrous Observing Wisdom (pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna) that illumines the pervasive and equal [Dharma-realm] is the illumination of Bodhisattvas.
The principle of emptiness reached therein is without ignorance and without darkness; it is the "illumination of non-illumination. Such are the three [illuminations] of the Tathāgata.
This is clear.

Next, regarding "one truth and one path": within the framework of the four truths of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), at the moment of the Vajra-mind on the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*), it coexists with Suffering and its Origin;
thus, there are three truths. Now, having reached the stage of Buddhahood, one is separated from those two and remains as only one—namely, the single path. Thus it is.

The single truth is pervasive, tranquil, and unobstructed; because the paths of all Buddhas are identical, it is called the "One Path. As a verse in a sutra says: "The Dharma of Mañjuśrī is ever thus;
the Dharma King has but one Dharma. All those who are unhindered give birth from the One Path and transcend birth and death."

Next, regarding the "unique dharma" (*ekadharmatā*): it is the virtue of the Great Self (*mahātman*), because it is without a second. It is called the virtue of Great Purity (*mahāśuddhaguṇa*). This is stated solely from the perspective of its category of meaning;

the previously mentioned virtue of purity was discussed because its meaning as a category of the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*) is proximate. Now, however, it is spoken of as the unique dharma from the standpoint of the Single Path (*ekamārga*).
Because the meanings of "one" (*eka*) and "solitary" (*kevala*) are similar, these four virtues are manifested by eliminating the four obstacles. As stated in the *Anuttarāśrayasūtra*:
"All arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas on the great stages are hindered from attaining the four virtues of the Tathāgata’s dharmakāya by four kinds of obstacles.
What are these four? First, the delusions that serve as conditions for birth; second, the delusions that serve as causes for birth."
Third is existence (*bhava*); fourth is non-existence (*abhava*). What is the delusion that serves as the condition for birth?

It is the ground of the abiding of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*), which gives rise to all formative forces (*saṃskāra*), just as ignorance gives rise to karma. What is the delusion that serves as the cause of birth?

It consists of all the formative forces produced by the ground of the abiding of ignorance, just like the various karmas produced by ignorance. What is existence? It is conditioned by the ground of the abiding of ignorance and caused by it.
The outflow-free (*anāsrava*) formations arising from the ground of the dwelling of ignorance (*avidyāvāsabhūmi*) give rise to the three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomayakāya*).

Just as, for example, with the four graspings (*upādāna*) as conditions and the three types of outflowing karma (*āsravakarma*) as causes, the three kinds of existence (*bhava*) arise; what is it that does not exist? It is that which, conditioned by the three kinds of mind-made bodies, [arises].
The subtle, imperceptible *anuśaya* (latent tendencies) that cease along with [the mind] are like the moment-to-moment aging and death that arise conditioned by the three realms of existence.

Because the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya*)—which is the locus of all afflictions—has not yet been severed, Arhats, Pratyekabuddhas, and even sovereign Bodhisattvas cannot attain the vision of the Great Pure Perfection (*mahā-viśuddhi-pāramitā*). This is due to ignorance.

Because the delusions of the signs of lightness arising from the Dwelling Grounds (*bhūmi*) have not been eliminated, and because the various aggregates of the mind-born (*manomaya-skandha*) produced by outflow-free karma (*anāsrava-karma*)—which arise with ignorance as their condition and subtle delusion as their cause—have not been fully exhausted, one cannot yet attain the vision of the *pāramitā* of Great Self (*mahātman*).
Furthermore, if one has not yet attained all... [the vision of the *pāramitā* of Great Bliss].
The afflictions, karmas, and births cannot be exhausted forever without remainder; these Tathāgatas are the realm of ambrosia (*amṛta-dhātu*).

They have severed the flow of death through transformation (*pariṇāmi-maraṇa*) and extinguished it immeasurably. There is no not-attaining the vision of the ultimate, unchanging Great Constant Perfection (*mahā-nitya-pāramitā*);

thus it is explained at length. Let us now set aside the discussion of the vehicle (*yāna*) and return to explaining the main text. Within the explanation of the fruit of the meaning, there are three parts.
Within the [three] divisions, the second—the detailed explanation—has already been concluded above.
From "All" onwards is the third, the summary. This consists of two sentences: first, the presentation of the result of the meaning; second, the conclusion that the paths are identical.

Within the detailed explanation of the result, there are three parts: first, the explanation of the result of the essence; second, the explanation of the result of the meaning. Thus are the two divisions.
It is ultimately as stated above. Regarding the second point—the third layer of the detailed exposition on the meaning of the essence—there are two fruits.

Within this, there are two parts: the specific exposition and the summary. In the first part, the specific exposition, the fruit of the essence is clarified first; herein, among ten phrases, the first five correctly clarify it.

The latter five constitute the conclusion. Regarding the first [of the initial five], the statement that "the essence of the fruit is perfected, such that there is no quality not cultivated and no principle not fully encompassed," refers to the gateway of the ultimate *dharmakāya*.
The second phrase, which states that it "abides in the pure land of the supreme truth (*paramārthasatya*) of the Middle Way," refers to the gateway of the *svasaṃbhogakāya* land.
The third phrase, which states "the infinite and the nameless," [refers to the gateway of the *nirmāṇakāya*].
Regarding "signlessness" (*animitta*): the pure land of the Dharma-body is the single Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), wherein all things are mutually interpenetrating and without limit;
thus it is called "infinite. Because the path of language is cut off, it is called "nameless. Because the sphere of mental activity has ceased, it is called "signless.
As for the fourth phrase, "not a single dharma can be apprehended": while all virtues are fully present, yet none...
Because all merits are ultimately unattainable. Regarding the fifth phrase, "neither having an essence nor lacking an essence":

although there is no single essence of a fruit, it is not that there is no single essence of a fruit. This is because the *dharmadhātu* is free from the nature of existence and non-existence, and thus all merits are mutually harmonious.
As the *Anuttarāśrayasūtra* states: "In all Buddha-fields, there is nothing whatsoever that constitutes an obstruction."
All Tathāgatas accord with equality; they have transcended the realm of conditioned activity and are devoid of conceptual characteristics.
Like space, they are without discrimination, for they are in perfect correspondence with the *dharmadhātu*. This section concludes the preceding [discussion] from the first [verse] through the third;

within it, there are five phrases arranged into three parts. The first two [phrases] conclude the preceding two [points] in forward order (*anuloma*), while the following two [phrases] conclude the subsequent [points] in reverse order (*pratiloma*).

There are two phrases. The third phrase concludes the intermediate section. "Single illumination" (*eka-avabhāsa*) concludes the statement that there is no virtue not perfected and no principle not universally encompassed;
for since every single merit is without exception illuminated, and principle and wisdom are in profound union, this too constitutes a single illumination.
"Single unified aspect" (*eka-saṃgata-lakṣaṇa*) concludes the statement regarding the Middle Way, the First Truth, and the Pure Land.
The Buddha and the Pure Land meet as non-dual; this is what is meant by abiding in the Middle Way land.

Regarding the characteristic of being of one essence (*ekatva-lakṣaṇa*), this concludes the fifth phrase: because it is not a substantial entity, it does not fall into non-substantiality; because it is not a non-substantial entity, it is not subject to substantiality.
Thus, it is directly the characteristic of being of one essence. Regarding the characteristic of singular awakening (*eka-bodhi-lakṣaṇa*), this concludes the fourth phrase: awakening to all...

The Dharma is identical to non-apprehension, for it is the characteristic of a single awakening. "Pure clarity is non-dual" refers to the phrase that, within the midst of bondage, there is no limit, no name, and no mark;
the pure land and the Buddha’s clarity are one and the same in their limitlessness. Furthermore, they are non-dual because they are free from names and marks.
This section on "Fruit" (phala) follows below to clarify the fruit of meaning (*arthaphala*). It consists of four parts: first, citing the fruit of essence to indicate the fruit of meaning;

second, revealing its distinctions based on the fruit of meaning; third, clarifying the intent behind establishing the fruit of meaning; and fourth, demonstrating the benefit of being able to understand the fruit of meaning.
Regarding the first part, the statement "this fruit is the solitary dharma, perfectly luminous, eternally abiding," reiterates the fruit of essence.
Furthermore, regarding the fact that the essence and characteristics of the single fruit have immeasurable meanings: this establishes meanings based upon the essence.

Regarding the fact that these meanings possess immeasurable virtues and these virtues possess immeasurable names: within each individual meaning there are immeasurable virtues, and within those virtues there are likewise immeasurable names.
The section beginning with "the fruit of meaning" is the second part, which reveals the distinctions. The term "Truth of Cessation" (nirodha-satya) is used to cite its pure virtues, such as bliss.

"Great Bliss" refers to the eternal; "the Dharma of Self" refers to the unique Dharma of the former [Buddhas]. This enumerates the final eighteen unshared qualities (*āveṇika-guṇa*) among the eighty-eight [qualities].
All these virtues collectively summarize the eighty-four categories previously explained. Regarding the term "fruit of fruits" (*phala-phala*):

it is because from the fruit of essence (*tattva-phala*) emerges the fruit of meaning (*artha-phala*). From here on, the third section establishes the intended meaning of all the names of the virtuous qualities. All...

Regarding "there is [the Buddha] because of teaching and transforming": this refers entirely to the gate of teaching and transforming sentient beings through the principle of the *nirmāṇakāya* (manifestation body) and *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body) of the *dharmakāya*.

It is by means of this that such names for the qualities of meaning are established. From the passage beginning with "If a worthy person" (*yady āryaḥ*) below, the fourth section demonstrates the benefits. "Worthy person" (*ārya*) refers to those on the three stages of worthiness (*traya-ārya*).
"All sentient beings" refers to ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who abide prior to these stages. If one can understand the meaning of these three phrases...

This is explained from the perspective of the gate of transformation and teaching. It is not that they exist as the words suggest; rather, because they have already attained the initial sprout of Buddhahood, they are prophesied by the Buddhas of the three periods of time.

Within the two sections that further clarify the two fruits, the first—specifically clarifying them—has already been concluded above. From "its fruit" onwards, the second section provides a general summary.
Regarding the statement that "its fruit is ineffable and unknowable": both its substantial fruit (*vastu-phala*) and its conceptual fruit (*artha-phala*) transcend all names and speech;
therefore, it is ineffable. Even the wisdom that follows after words cannot know it. It is merely [described] according to the names and characteristics of sentient beings.

The Dharma is expressed through provisional designations that characterize the nature and meaning of its essence; thus, by means of words, one speaks of the dharmas of names and characteristics within the context of those very names and characteristics.
Below, the distinctions between the two fruits of these provisional designations are revealed.

Within the Buddha’s response, there are two parts. The first concludes the specific explanation of the meaning of cause and effect. From "I have taught" onwards is the second part, which provides the summary conclusion.
○ Chapter on the Great Assembly Receiving and Studying the Teaching.
Within the section on the "Correct Exposition," there are two parts. The first, the section where the Tathāgata expounds for them, is now concluded.

Below this is the second part, concerning the assembly’s reception and study. "Reception" refers to receiving the precepts; "study" refers to practicing the conduct. Without rising from one's seat, they receive the ten precepts.
One continues to study the six sense bases from beginning to end; this section clarifies that meaning, hence it is called the "Chapter on Receiving Instruction.

The text consists of two parts: first, the question, and second, the answer. Within the question, there are also two parts: first, the preface stating the purpose of the ritual, and second, the formal posing of the questions.
Within the posing of the questions, the preceding inquiry is acknowledged before the subsequent ones are raised.
The response consists of four parts: first, emitting light to assemble the multitude, for the purpose of providing witness to the fact that [the teaching] was received and learned while seated once;
second, praising the inquiry and exhorting study, wherein the seven bodhisattvas are addressed because they are the presiding masters of the seven assemblies in the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra.

The phrase "one who is able to inquire about the three contemplations" indicates that among the questions posed, one is to receive instruction and cultivate the path; the term "cultivating the path" is used because it reveals the cultivation of the three contemplations.

Next, the phrase "the path of the self-nature purity of all Buddhas of the dharma-realm" indicates the sentence within the inquiry concerning the complete practice of each stage from beginning to end.
Next, the phrase "the dharma of the clear contemplation cultivated by all Bodhisattvas" [indicates the inquiry regarding the specific methods].

The "gate" refers to the phrase indicating the sequential entry into the stage of a bodhisattva for one who asks [this question]. Furthermore, regarding these three phrases, the first is general and the latter two are specific.
As for the first being general, it refers to the "three contemplations," which collectively present the terminology for receiving instruction and practicing the Path.
As for the latter being specific, the second phrase specifically clarifies the term "Path," and the third phrase specifically clarifies the term "practice. From the words "You all... onwards...
The exhortation to study may be understood from this. "O Son of the Buddha, I shall now speak further" constitutes the third section, the promise to teach.

"If all sentient beings... constitutes the fourth section, the actual response. This [fourth section] contains two parts: the specific response and the general response. Within the first of these, there are also two parts.

First, the reception; second, the training. Within the reception, there are three parts: the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion. The "heading" refers to citing faith as the basis for receiving the precepts, because one must first give rise to faith before receiving the precepts.
From "The Initial Practice" onwards is the second part, the extensive explanation. This contains four sections: first, the ritual procedure for receiving the precepts;
second, from "The Buddha said" onwards, the preparatory methods for receiving the precepts, which itself contains three sub-sections, the first of which is... [the first of the three].
One pays homage to the Three Jewels; next, one respectfully accepts the Four Reliances; and finally, one immediately repents of transgressions.

If one were to follow the *karmavācanā* for receiving precepts according to the Hīnayāna, the respectful acceptance of the Four Refuges within this context should be considered the actual conferral of the precepts.

However, judging by the force of the textual flow of this sūtra, this passage on respectful acceptance is not the formal conferral of the precepts, because it would be illogical to repent after having already received them. Therefore, this text is so judged.
This serves as a preparatory expedient. Thus, the third section below clarifies the formal conferral of the precepts. This section contains three parts:

first, restating the previous confession of transgressions and marking the commencement of the formal bestowal; second, the formal conferral of the ten precepts; and third, the concluding praise of the virtue of the precepts.
These three points together constitute the third section, which clarifies the meaning of the text for the formal conferral of the precepts.

Regarding the fourth section, the analysis through various categories beginning with "past and future," it is said that there is a method for receiving the dharma but no method for relinquishing it; that is, one may incur an offense yet not lose [the vow], maintaining it until the end of the future.
As stated in the *Viniscaya-saṃgrahaṇī* of the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*: "If one does not relinquish such a discipline, it should be known that..."
It may also continue to function in subsequent lives; it is not something that is relinquished by those [lives]. Furthermore, there are briefly four kinds of causes and conditions for relinquishing:
first, the definitive arousal of a mind of undertaking that is of a different category [from the previous state];
second, intentionally uttering words of renunciation in the presence of a discerning person of integrity; third, the general or specific violation of the four types of defeats (*parājika*).

Dharma. Fourth, if one commits a total or partial transgression through the most intense degree of entanglement (*paryavasthāna*), thereby conforming to the four kinds of dharmas that lead to being overcome by others, one should know that by this cause and condition, the bodhisattva vows are relinquished.
If there is a restoration of purity through a renewed resolve, one should receive them again. Thus, how are the treatise and this sutra to be reconciled? The explanation says: "That..."

In the teachings of the Three Vehicles, there is the fault of abandoning the Dharma and violating the precepts, because the bodhicitta generated by a bodhisattva based on those teachings is incomplete and not firm.
This present sutra, however, is the teaching of the One Vehicle; therefore, there is no such fault of abandoning the Dharma or violating the precepts.
Generating the mind of awakening in reliance upon this is the opposite of what was previously maintained. Let us now conclude the discussion of the vehicles and return [to our original subject].
To explain the main text: from the passage "At that time, among the assembly... onwards, this is the third summary of receiving the precepts.

"Rising from one's seat to receive and uphold the Buddha’s precepts" means that the act of receiving the precepts begins at this very sitting; it is because one does not rise from this seat that one enters the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
Regarding the names below, the second section clarifies training (*śikṣā*). This contains two parts: a detailed explanation and a general explanation.

Within the detailed explanation, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are clarified. In each passage concerning the six sense bases, there are two sentences: first, the state of the sense base is clarified; second, the practice of training is revealed.
The initial statement that one enters the stage of the first dwelling (*prathamā bhūmi*) by fulfilling the cultivation of the ten precepts clarifies the entry into the stages.

From here on, the subsequent practice is further elucidated. Regarding the "ten faiths" (*daśa-śraddhā*), as stated in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*: "Bodhisattvas possess ten kinds of indestructible faith (*akṣaya-śraddhā*).
What are these ten? They are: indestructible faith in all Buddhas; indestructible faith in all Buddha-dharmas; [and so forth].
Unwavering faith: unwavering faith in all noble Saṅghas; unwavering faith in all bodhisattvas; unwavering faith in all spiritual friends;
unwavering faith in all sentient beings; unwavering faith in all the great vows of bodhisattvas;
unwavering faith in all the practices of bodhisattvas; [unwavering faith] in honoring and making offerings to one...

They possess indestructible faith in all Buddhas; they possess indestructible faith in the skillful means for accomplishing the teaching and transformation of all sentient beings and the realization of bodhisattvahood.
These are the ten kinds. Regarding the "ten advances," there are ten kinds of diligence for a bodhisattva, namely:
diligence in purifying physical action, because of never regressing in reverently making offerings to all Buddhas; diligence in verbal action... [and so forth].
Vigor of mental action consists in extensively explaining the Dharma as it has been heard to others without weariness.

Upright vigor consists in skillfully entering the meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*), liberations (*vimokṣa*), and samādhis of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity, continuing them without regression.
It is far removed from deceit and crookedness, being upright in all skillful means because it ultimately never regresses.
It is the vigor of the profound mind, constantly tending toward the superior realms and accumulating unsurpassed wisdom and pure dharmas.

It is the practice of non-false vigor, which encompasses generosity, ethical discipline, patience, and extensive learning, as well as heedfulness, until reaching the site of enlightenment without ceasing midway. It excludes...
The diligence of subduing all māras and adversaries is able to utterly eliminate the afflictions of the three poisons, wrong views, and all entanglements and hindrances.
The diligence of fulfilling the light of wisdom ensures that whatever is undertaken is preceded by thorough reflection, so that the mind does not experience regret midway.
Because they bring all matters to ultimate completion, they possess the diligence of non-attachment;

because they transcend the realm of the mind and the characteristics or non-characteristics of body, speech, and mind, they possess the diligence of the light of Dharma through the profoundly deep Dharma-gates.

Thus, they fully accomplish the light of Dharma and progressively enter all the stages (*bhūmi*), even manifesting the relinquishing of celestial lifespan, descending into the world, leaving the household life, attaining enlightenment, turning the wheel of Dharma, and entering *nirvāṇa*.

Because they are the basis [for practice], these constitute the ten types. The ten "aspirations for advancement" (prasthāna) refer to the ten recollections (*daśa-smṛti*); because one advances toward the Buddha, Dharma, and so forth through these recollections.
The ten "vehicles" (*yāna*) refer to the ten wisdoms (*daśa-prajñā*); because wisdom is supreme for removing obstructions and bringing about transcendence. The ten "vajras" refer to the ten dhyānas;
because they maintain the object of focus in tranquil concentration without any disruption. The ten "rejoicings" (*anumodanā*) refer to...
The ten acts of giving (*daśa-dāna*). Because those who receive [the gift] with sympathetic joy (*anumodana*) obtain benefit. Regarding the "ten protections" (*daśa-rakṣā*):

these refer to the ten kinds of abandoning demonic activities (*mārakarman*), for by abandoning demonic activities one protects the Buddha-dharma. Within each of these ten sets, the ten recollections (*daśa-smṛti*) and ten vows (*daśa-praṇidhāna*) appear in the "Chapter on the Ten Grounds" (*Daśabhūmika-parivarta*);
the remaining eight gates appear in the "Chapter on Leaving the World" (*Lokottara-parivarta*). Those who wish to practice them in full should seek them therein. As...
This sequence of entering into practice, entering toward [the goal], and entering the stages (*bhūmi*) may be understood as follows.

Regarding the statement in the *Vimalā-bhūmi* that "the consciousness of all sentient beings initially arises as a single characteristic and abides in its object," this is spoken in terms of coarse characteristics. Consciousness is of three grades:

the coarsest and most superficial is the so-called sixfold consciousness (*ṣaḍvijñāna*); the intermediate grade is called the manas; and the subtle grade of consciousness is the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*).
It is called "initial arising" because it is the source of all consciousnesses. Within this initial consciousness, there are three subtle aspects, namely:

the aspect of karma (*karmalakṣaṇa*), the aspect of transformation (*pravṛttilakṣaṇa*), and the aspect of manifestation (*nirbhāsalakṣaṇa*). These three aspects appear in the *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna*.

What is here termed the "single aspect of initial arising" is precisely the aspect of karma. Because the intrinsically pure mind is moved by the wind of ignorance, this is the first aspect of karma; therefore, it is called the "one aspect. One.
Once the characteristic has moved, it must necessarily depend upon causes and conditions; for this reason, it is said to "abide in conditions.
This single characteristic possesses two functions: first, the function of clear discernment, and second, the function of deluded confusion.

Just as when the waters of the great ocean rise into waves, they do not lose their nature of clarity and thus accord with their original purity, one should know that the discerning function within consciousness is likewise so: even when moving, it does not lose [its nature].

The nature of original enlightenment (*prakṛti-āśraya*) is precisely the meaning of original enlightenment as it conforms to defilement. As the sūtra states, because names arise in accordance with the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), they are termed "wholesome" (*kuśala*).
Furthermore, just as water possesses the function of turbidity when it moves, one should know that the function of delusion within consciousness is likewise so.

As the sūtra states, because names arise in opposition to the ultimate truth, they are termed "afflictions" (*kleśa*). These two are called "innate" (*upapatti-labdha*) because they serve as the basis. Their...

Regarding "arising": all [states] function as acquisitions through cultivation (*prāyogika*) or acquisition through birth (*upapattilābhika*). Alternatively, one may give rise to a mind associated with the three realms. Regarding these acquisitions through birth, there is further the function of delusion;

one fails to understand that the minds associated with the three realms which have arisen are empty. These three functions of delusion still reside within the fundamental consciousness (*mūlavijñāna*);

therefore, it is said that this constitutes "abiding" in the stage of acquisition. That [acquisition] is one acquired through birth, while these are three acquired through cultivation; these four serve as the basis for giving rise to all afflictions.
Regarding "affliction": as the sūtra states, because all afflictions arise from these four grounds of abiding (*catur-vāsabhūmi*), they are established as the initial four grounds of abiding.

These four grounds of abiding do not function through clear comprehension; they lack the distinction between coarse and subtle aspects of activity, and are therefore collectively termed the "ground of beginningless ignorance" (*anādikālikā-avidyā-vāsabhūmi*).
As the sūtra says: "Prior to these four grounds of abiding, no other latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) can arise"; for this reason, it is called "beginningless ignorance."
Because they abide in the stages (*bhūmi*). These four stages have the single mind as their root, and the two kinds of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) as their branches.
At the time of the diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*), one knows that the branches will eventually end, yet has not yet reached the principle of the root, the single mind.

Therefore, it is said that one knows this initial arising of the single characteristic has an end, but does not know its beginning. Whether there were previously dharmas or no dharmas—even this is known only by the Buddha.
Because it is from beginning to end. The remaining passages may be understood by analogy with this.

"O Son of the Buddha, what I have said" and so forth is the second section, which summarizes the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). This contains four parts: first, a summary stating that there is no entry among the six sense bases that does not occur;
second, a specific summary regarding those who do not arise from this seat and enter [the path]; third, "I, from the beginning... and so forth; [and fourth, the conclusion].
The third [section] was a summary of the entries into the seven locations of the *Avataṃsaka*. Now, with this fourth [section], we again conclude the entries into this specific assembly.
Within the three divisions of this entire scripture, the second—the main exposition—has already been completed above.

○ Chapter on Gathering and Dispersing. This is the third section, the Section on Circulation (*parīndanā*). It consists of two parts in the text: first, the exhortation to uphold and circulate [the teaching]; second, the demonstration of the method for circulation.
Within the first part, there are also two sections: (1) the exhortation to uphold and receive the teaching for circulation; and (2) the manifestation of light for re-exhortation.

Exhortation to Circulate. Regarding the second [section], it says: "The beginner practitioner who enters the nine stages of contemplative absorption" refers to one who has come from the third fruit of the path up to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), as they have now begun to enter the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*).
As for the "seven purities," the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "What are called the seven kinds of purity? First, purity of ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*);
second, purity of mind; third, purity of view; fourth, purity through the overcoming of doubt; fifth, knowledge of what is the path and what is not the path..."

He sees. He possesses the knowledge of the vision of the six knowledges (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā-jñāna-darśana*). He possesses the knowledge of the vision of the abandonment of the seven courses of action (*sapta-karma-patha-prahāṇa-jñāna-darśana*).

Regarding what herein constitutes the path and the non-path: the path is that which is preceded by right view; the non-path is that which is preceded by wrong view. To understand, as they truly are, the courses of action and the abandonment of those courses, one understands, as they truly are, the four types of tracks (*catur-vidha-yāna*).

What are these four? First, the track of painful practice with slow progress (*duḥkhā pratipat dhandhābhijñā*); second, the track of painful practice with quick progress (*duḥkhā pratipat kṣiprābhijñā*); third, [the track of pleasant practice with slow progress]; fourth, [the track of pleasant practice with quick progress].
The practice with ease and slow progress; the four practices with ease and quick progress.

Regarding these, one should understand them as the foremost and initial tracks for the purpose of transcending all that is to be abandoned, rather than for the purpose of dissociation from the afflictions (*kleśa*). One should know this as it truly is.

One should know that in the second and third [tracks], a portion is to be abandoned. Having thus understood that the entirety of the first and a portion of the second and third should be abandoned, one relies upon...

The joy of swift penetration is achieved through the right exertion of cultivation; because from this, one immediately and forever exhausts all outflows (*āsrava*), it is said here that the ten precepts constitute the first purity.
The mind entering meditative concentration is the second purity. The vision of the Path is the third purity.
Crossing over doubt is the fourth purity. The Right Path is the fifth purity. This is the knowledge of conduct and insight.
This is the sixth purity. Practicing the knowledge and vision of cessation is the seventh purity. By means of these seven purities, one enters the Mahāyāna;
therefore, it is said that one "attains entry into the Dharma."
From "At that time" onwards is the second section, the method for the dissemination [of the teaching]. This contains four parts: first, the question; second, the answer;
third, the expression of lamentation; and fourth, the practice and observance. The textual characteristics of these are readily apparent.

Chapter One: The Gathering of the Assembly. The Buddha again visited the tree at the site of enlightenment and emitted forty-two rays of light.
He gathered ten bodhisattvas from the ten forest realms, who had come from the presence of the Buddha Ten-Vigor; he also gathered all the hosts of devas and others.

Chapter Two: On the Names of the Sages and Holy Ones. This section explains the names of the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*), the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*), equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), and wondrous enlightenment (*vicitra-bodhi*).
In all cases, both the Chinese and Sanskrit terms are presented together.

It further explains the ten mental states prior to abiding—namely, faith, thought, diligence, concentration, wisdom, precepts, dedication, protection of the Dharma, relinquishment, and aspiration. It also presents twenty-four verses on vows, and further discusses the ten non-... [the text continues].

The Precepts Subject to Confession. Chapter Three: The Noble Disciples’ Contemplation. The ten stages of abiding (*daśa-vihāra*) are called the stage of cultivated nature (*śikṣā-bhūmi*). The ten stages of practice (*daśa-caryā*) are called the stage of innate nature (*prakṛti-bhūmi*).

The ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*) are called the stage of the path-nature (*mārga-bhūmi*). The ten stages of the bodhisattva grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*) are called the stage of noble nature (*ārya-bhūmi*). Next is the stage of equal enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi-bhūmi*), followed by the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*suviśuddha-bodhi-bhūmi*).

Nature. It is also called the six firmnesses (*ṣaḍ-dārḍhya*), the six patiences (*ṣaḍ-kṣānti*), the six wisdoms (*ṣad-prajñā*), the six concentrations (*ṣad-samādhi*), the six contemplations (*ṣad-vipaśyanā*), and the six-jeweled necklace (*ṣad-ratna-hāra*).
These are: first, the copper jewel; second, the silver jewel; third, the gold jewel; fourth, the lapis lazuli jewel;
fifth, the maṇi jewel; and sixth, the crystal jewel. Furthermore, it explains the various practices cultivated during these six stages. (End of above)

Chapter Four, "Explanation of Meanings," further explains the meanings of the ten prior faiths and the forty-two stages.
Chapter Five, "The Mother of Buddhas," answers the Bodhisattva Gajapramukha’s inquiry regarding the meaning of the two truths, and also describes the small, medium, and great kalpas.

Chapter Six: The Chapter on Cause and Effect. This explains that each of the ten *pāramitās* possesses three conditions;

furthermore, it teaches that the seven riches, the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*), and the four reliances (*pratisaraṇa*) serve as the causes, while the two kinds of *dharmakāya* constitute the results.
Chapter Seven: The Great Assembly Accepting and Studying the Precepts The Buddha again emitted light to assemble the multitude.

He entrusted Mañjuśrī, Sudhana, and seven other great bodhisattvas, each to lead a portion of the assembly to accept and study the teachings. Thereupon, he distinguished the three types of receiving the precepts as well as the ritual procedures for receiving them.

Through the reception of these precepts, [the practitioners] gradually enter the stages of *chū* (abiding), *xíng* (practice), *xiàng* (orientation), and the *dì* (grounds), culminating in the stage of Wondrous Enlightenment (*mìojiào*).
Chapter Eight: Gathering and Dispersing. Third, he exhorts the great assembly to resolve upon Bodhicitta.
Furthermore, he repeatedly instructs that one must first receive the Bodhisattva precepts before this great Dharma-gate may be explained to them.
The above is excerpted from the thirty-second fascicle of the *Yue zang zhi jin* (Guide to the Sutra Repository), within the section on the Mahāyāna Vinaya Piṭaka.
Regarding the two-fascicle *Buddhabhāṣita Brahmajāla Sūtra* listed above, Master Suguo commented: "This sūtra was originally part of the same collection as the *Avataṃsaka*.
Since the 'Chapter on Nature' (*Xing pin*) now circulates independently, both the Northern and Southern Tripitakas have classified it [separately]."

[The *Vinaya* (referred to as "this sutra" below)] This work also appears to be included within the Avataṃsaka division. Master Zhizhe relied upon it to delineate the sequence of stages [in the *Fahua Xuanyi*].
Now, because it elucidates from beginning to end the ten grave precepts (*daśa-śīlāni*), both the Northern and Southern traditions alike classify it within the Vinaya Piṭaka.
